name: Herbert Lee
summary: Herbert Lee, 52, a farmer and NAACP voter-registration organizer who worked closely with SNCC activist Bob Moses, was shot and killed at Westbrook's Cotton Gin in Liberty on September 25, 1961, by Mississippi state representative E.H. Hurst. Hurst said the two men argued over a debt and that Lee swung a tire iron at him, prompting Hurst to strike him with a pistol, which discharged and killed him. A coroner's inquest, held inside the cotton gin office within an hour of the shooting, found Hurst acted in self-defense; witnesses, including Lee's friend Louis Allen, corroborated Hurst's account under oath. Two justices of the peace subsequently declined to send the case to a grand jury, and Hurst was released the same day he was charged. Louis Allen later told the FBI he had lied at the inquest out of fear, and that Lee had not actually threatened Hurst. Allen was harassed for years afterward and was murdered in 1964, shortly before he planned to leave Mississippi — a killing documented separately in this archive.
known: Victim identity, background, and the September 25, 1961 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file.

A coroner's inquest and two justices of the peace concluded Hurst acted in self-defense and declined to refer the case to a grand jury; the corroborating witness, Louis Allen, later told the FBI he had lied out of fear, per the same file.
unknown: Whether Lee actually threatened Hurst with a tire iron, as multiple witnesses testified under oath at the time, was directly contradicted by at least one of those same witnesses years later.
No one was ever convicted in Lee's death.
unanswered: What specifically caused Louis Allen to recant his corroborating testimony to the FBI, and what protection, if any, was he offered in exchange?
What connection exists between this case and Louis Allen's own unsolved 1964 murder, committed after he began cooperating with federal investigators?
What became of the other witnesses who testified alongside Allen at the original 1961 inquest?

name: Samuel Younge Jr.
summary: Samuel Younge Jr., 21, a Navy veteran, civil rights activist, and freshman at Tuskegee Institute, was fatally shot beneath the left eye by 68-year-old gas station attendant Marvin Segrest just before midnight on January 3, 1966, after an argument over Younge's use of a whites-only restroom. Segrest was arrested the next day, indicted for second-degree murder by a Macon County grand jury, and released on $20,000 bond. His shooting set off a demonstration in Tuskegee attended by roughly 2,000 students and faculty. At trial in December 1966, forensic testimony indicated the fatal shot had been fired from several feet away, contradicting any claim of a close struggle. An all-white jury in Lee County acquitted Segrest after deliberating for 71 minutes.
known: Victim identity, background, and the January 3, 1966 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file.
Marvin Segrest was indicted for second-degree murder and tried, but was acquitted by an all-white jury after 71 minutes of deliberation in December 1966, per the same file.
unknown: No one was ever convicted in Younge's death.
The medical examiner's finding that the fatal shot came from several feet away was never reconciled with any account of a close physical struggle.
unanswered: What specific evidence or arguments led the jury to acquit despite the forensic distance findings?
What became of the roughly 2,000-person demonstration's broader effect on civil rights organizing at Tuskegee Institute?
What additional trial transcript detail, if any, has been preserved beyond the summary in the DOJ's file?

name: Isaiah Taylor
summary: Isaiah Taylor, who had a documented history of mental health problems, was shot and killed on the side of Highway 49 near Ruleville on the afternoon of June 26, 1964, by Mississippi Highway Patrol Patrolman Robert Wallace. Wallace said he and a local constable were searching for an escaped state penitentiary inmate when they came upon Taylor standing beside the road, covering his face with his hands. According to Wallace's account, when he approached and questioned him, a confrontation followed that ended in the shooting. No independent civilian witnesses to the encounter were ever identified. No charges were ever filed against Wallace, and the case was closed decades later after the DOJ determined both Wallace and the constable present were deceased.
known: Victim identity and the June 26, 1964 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file.
No independent civilian witnesses to the shooting were ever identified, and no charges were filed against Patrolman Robert Wallace, per the same file.
unknown: The specific sequence of events between Wallace's approach and the shooting itself rests entirely on Wallace's own account.
Whether Taylor's documented mental health history played any role in the encounter was never independently examined.
unanswered: What became of the escaped penitentiary inmate Wallace and the constable were reportedly searching for that day?
Why were no independent witnesses to the roadside encounter ever located, given the highway setting?
What internal Mississippi Highway Patrol review, if any, followed the shooting?

name: Maceo Snipes
summary: Maceo Snipes, 37, a World War II veteran who had fought in New Guinea, was shot in the back on July 18, 1946, one day after becoming the first and only Black resident of Taylor County to vote in that year's Georgia Democratic primary, despite explicit threats from the Ku Klux Klan and a public warning from a former governor that “wise Negroes will stay away from the white folks' ballot boxes.” Four white men, led by Edward Williamson, drove to the farmhouse where Snipes lived with his mother and grandfather and called him outside; Williamson shot him and the men drove away. Snipes died two days later after the hospital treating him said no blood was available for a needed transfusion. A coroner's jury acquitted Williamson on a self-defense claim, despite Snipes's own deathbed statement and his mother's witness testimony contradicting it. Fearing retaliation, the family buried him secretly at night in a grave whose location remains unknown to his surviving relatives, and much of the family fled the county. Snipes's killing, alongside the Moore's Ford lynchings that occurred in Georgia just one week later, prompted a young Morehouse College student, Martin Luther King Jr., to write a public letter condemning the state's racial violence. No one was ever held accountable.
known: Victim identity, background, and the July 17–20, 1946 timeline, per the DOJ's public case file, PBS FRONTLINE's “Un(re)solved” case summary, and the Georgia Civil Rights Cold Cases Project at Emory University.
A coroner's jury acquitted Edward Williamson on a self-defense claim on July 29, 1946, despite contradicting deathbed and eyewitness testimony; no one was ever held accountable, per the same sources.
unknown: No one was ever convicted in Snipes's death.
The exact location of Snipes's grave, buried secretly at night out of fear for the family's safety, remains unknown even to his surviving relatives.
unanswered: What did the FBI's investigation, requested by the DOJ after Williamson's acquittal, ultimately establish?

What connection, if any, exists between this case and Isaiah Nixon's killing two years later in nearby Montgomery County, documented separately in this archive — both killings tied to voting, both resulting in acquittals, both driving surviving families out of the region?
What became of the 2006 push by the NAACP and the Prison & Jail Project for a renewed federal investigation?

name: James Earl Motley
summary: James Earl Motley, 27, died from head injuries in the Elmore County jail around 3:30 a.m. on November 20, 1966, hours after Deputy Harvey Conner stopped the car he was riding in for a traffic violation. When Motley told Conner he lacked jurisdiction because the stop had occurred in a different county, Conner ordered him out of the car; witnesses said Conner then struck Motley repeatedly in the head with a slapjack, and that state troopers who arrived as backup held Motley by the arms while he was beaten. Conner took the bleeding Motley to the county jail, where local authorities said he fell twice and struck his head before losing consciousness. An autopsy found multiple skull fractures and brain hemorrhage; a coroner concluded the fatal injury could have come from the beating, the falls, or some combination, and classified the death as “accidental.” A state grand jury declined to indict Conner on a homicide charge in January 1967. He was separately tried in federal court for violating Motley's civil rights; an all-white jury with one Black member returned a not-guilty verdict on April 12, 1967.
known: Victim identity and the November 20, 1966 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file and PBS FRONTLINE's “Un(re)solved” case summary.
A state grand jury declined to indict Deputy Harvey Conner, and a subsequent federal jury acquitted him in April 1967; the coroner classified Motley's death as accidental, per the same sources.
unknown: No one was ever held criminally accountable for Motley's death.
Whether the fatal head injury resulted from the beating, the falls at the jail, or some combination was never conclusively determined.
unanswered: What specific testimony from the two incarcerated men who carried Motley into his cell was presented at either the grand jury or the federal trial?
What became of the state troopers who reportedly held Motley by the arms during the beating?
What additional detail, if any, survives in the original 1966 Alabama Department of Public Safety investigative file?

name: Thad Christian
summary: Thad Christian, 54, was fatally shot in the abdomen with a shotgun on August 30, 1965, while fishing with a friend at a creek in the rural community of Central City, west of Anniston. Robert Haynes, 41, had earlier told the two men to leave the area without saying whether he owned the property, then returned and shot Christian as they loaded their fishing gear into their car. Haynes was arrested and charged with murder, but pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of first-degree manslaughter and was sentenced to five years at a prison camp; how much of that sentence he actually served was not documented. Haynes died in a car accident three years later, in 1968. When the FBI reopened the case decades afterward, it found most surviving local records had been damaged by water and were illegible; one salvaged 1965 file noted a claim that several other Black men had also been at the creek that afternoon, a detail never further investigated.
known: Victim identity, background, and the August 30, 1965 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file and PBS FRONTLINE's “Un(re)solved” case summary.
Robert Haynes pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter and was sentenced to five years, a fraction of the murder charge originally filed; he died in 1968, per the same sources.
unknown: How much of his five-year sentence Haynes actually served before his 1968 death was never documented.
The identities of the other Black men reportedly present at the creek that afternoon, referenced in a 1965 FBI file, were never established.
unanswered: Why was a murder charge reduced to first-degree manslaughter, and what plea negotiation led to that outcome?
Who were the other men reportedly at the creek, and might any of them have left surviving accounts?
What became of the original Calhoun County court records before they were damaged beyond legibility?

name: Isaiah Henry
summary: Isaiah Henry, 38, a school bus driver and farmer who helped his Black neighbors prepare for voter registration tests, was found severely beaten on the side of a road in St. Helena Parish on July 28, 1954, one day after he voted in the Democratic primary. Unidentified men had called on him that morning and he left with them; he was later taken to a hospital in New Orleans. In early August 1954, sheriff's office deputies arrested a local police juror, Lester Hornsby, and a sheriff's deputy, Carl Womak, on charges of simple kidnapping and attempted murder; Womak had been the deputy assigned to the polling place where Henry voted. A contemporaneous news article quoted the assistant district attorney saying the two men were held because he believed they knew something about the beating, but no record indicates either man was ever indicted. Local jail logbooks, arrest warrants, and prosecutorial files from the case no longer exist. One of Henry's sons later said his father was likely beaten because of his political involvement.
known: Victim identity, background, and the July 27–28, 1954 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file, drawing on a 2007 article in The Advocate.
Lester Hornsby and Carl Womak were arrested on kidnapping and attempted murder charges in connection with the case, but no record indicates either was ever indicted, per the same file.
unknown: No one was ever convicted in connection with Henry's beating.
The full circumstances of his abduction that morning, and what happened to him before he was found on the roadside, were never documented.
unanswered: Why were Hornsby and Womak never indicted despite being arrested and held specifically because officials believed they knew something about the beating?
What became of the original St. Helena Parish jail logbooks and investigative files before they were lost?
What connection, if any, existed between Henry's beating and his broader work helping neighbors prepare for voter registration tests?

name: John Earl Reese
summary: John Earl Reese, 16, was shot and killed on the night of October 22, 1955, while dancing with his cousins in a café in Mayflower, a small Black community near Longview. Perry Dean Ross, driving roughly 85 miles per hour, fired nine shots from a rifle into the café window as his car passed; Reese was killed, and two of his cousins were wounded. The same night, gunmen fired into at least one other home in the area where Black residents lived. The attacks were tied to local anger over a bond election to build a new school for Black children following the Brown v. Board of Education decision; Ross later admitted his anger over the new school had “a great deal” to do with the shooting. The local sheriff initially refused to investigate, insisting Black residents were responsible for their own community's shooting. Texas Rangers eventually interviewed over 300 people and identified Ross and a second man, Joe Simpson, both of whom confessed. Simpson's charges were dropped in exchange for his testimony against Ross, who was convicted of murder in April 1957 and given a two-to-five-year sentence that was immediately suspended; Simpson later pleaded guilty to the same charge and received an identical suspended sentence. Neither man served any time in prison.
known: Victim identity and the October 22, 1955 date and circumstances, per the DOJ's public case file and extensive contemporaneous and historical reporting.
Perry Dean Ross and Joe Simpson both confessed and were convicted, but both received fully suspended sentences and served no prison time, per the same sources.
unknown: Whether the other shootings that same night at additional homes were connected to the same group of men was never conclusively established.
The full scope of who else may have been involved in planning the night's attacks beyond Ross and Simpson was never investigated.
unanswered: Why did the local sheriff initially refuse to investigate despite the shooting's obvious severity?
What became of the broader dispute over the new school's location that the Texas Rangers identified as the underlying motive?
Why were fully suspended sentences considered appropriate for two confessed killers in a case the district attorney himself urged the jury to punish severely?

name: Frank Andrews
summary: Frank Andrews, 27, was shot in the back and killed on November 28, 1964 outside Smith's Café in Lisman, Alabama, by Quinnie Donald, a white Choctaw County sheriff's chief deputy. Donald and another deputy said they were at the café, which served the local Black community, investigating illegal whiskey; Donald claimed Andrews advanced on a fellow deputy with a knife, a claim disputed by witness accounts. A local grand jury declined to indict, and no one was ever prosecuted for his death.
known: Victim identity, age, and the November 28, 1964 shooting outside Smith's Café in Lisman, per the Department of Justice's Cold Case closing memorandum.
The shooter, sheriff's chief deputy Quinnie Donald, was publicly identified in the DOJ memo and in FBI records reviewed by PBS Frontline's Unresolved project.
A local grand jury declined to indict Donald in 1964, and no state or federal charges were ever brought.
unknown: Whether Andrews in fact drew a knife, as Donald claimed, is disputed — the three eyewitnesses identified in 1964 gave factually inconsistent accounts, per the DOJ memo.

In a 2008 re-interview under the Till Act, Donald reportedly gave an account of the shooting that conflicted with what he told investigators in 1964; the full substance of that shift is not detailed in the public record.
unanswered: What specifically changed between Donald's 1964 and 2008 accounts of the shooting, and why?
Why did the three 1964 eyewitness accounts conflict, and was that inconsistency investigated further at the time?
What led the FBI and DOJ to close the reopened case in 2013 without prosecution, given the disputed record?

name: Alexis Patterson
summary: Alexis Patterson, 7, disappeared on the morning of May 3, 2002 after her stepfather walked her to a crosswalk roughly half a block from Hi-Mount Community School in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and a crossing guard escorted her across the street. She never arrived in her first-grade classroom; classmates later reported seeing her crying on the playground before and after the school day. Her disappearance prompted one of the largest search efforts in Milwaukee police history, but no arrests have ever been made and Alexis has never been found.
known: Victim identity, age, and the May 3, 2002 disappearance near Hi-Mount Community School, per the FBI's public case listing and the Milwaukee Police Department.
Her stepfather told police he watched her cross the street toward the school playground before he walked home; the school reported she never attended class that day.
The Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office has offered a $10,000 reward for information leading to her return, and the FBI continues to list her as an open case.
unknown: What happened to Alexis between being seen on the playground and her confirmed absence from class has never been publicly established.
No suspect has ever been officially named by police.
Full results of the searches of the Milwaukee River and other sites are not comprehensively public.
unanswered: What, if anything, did the reported 2003 John Doe investigation — never officially confirmed by police — establish?
What has the Milwaukee Police Department's cold case unit found in its ongoing review, if anything?
Why does a documented gap remain between witness accounts of Alexis's morning and her confirmed disappearance?

name: Nacomie Freeman
summary: Nacomie Freeman, 24, was shot in the stomach and pushed out of a moving truck in the 1600 block of West Denton Avenue in Phoenix, Arizona, on June 24, 2004. Witnesses reported seeing her pushed from a dark-colored, late-1990s-model short-bed truck; she was pronounced dead at the scene. The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office has said investigators developed some leads but have never made an arrest.

The attackers fled immediately, and the case has remained unsolved since.

summary: Julius Dubouse, 45, died in Anchorage, Alaska in the early morning hours of December 3, 1998, after an accelerant was thrown through the back window of his residence. The Anchorage Police Department's Cold Case Section, whose mission is to systematically review unsolved deaths in its jurisdiction, lists his death among its open homicide investigations. No arrest has ever been made.

name: Kierre Davies
summary: Kierre Davies, 27, was shot and killed alongside his friend and fellow rapper, 28-year-old Jaquan Gatewood, in the early morning hours of November 19, 2022, outside a house near the North Dakota State University campus in Fargo. Both men were at a gathering at the home; neither lived there. Police say everyone involved knew each other and have said there is no danger to the public, but more than a year later no arrest has been made and the case remains open.
known: Victim identity, age, and the November 19, 2022 shooting near NDSU, per Fargo Police Department statements and local news coverage.
Davies and Gatewood, both local rappers, were shot together at a gathering neither of them hosted; police say the men involved were known to each other.
A search warrant later revealed a gun was found in Gatewood's hand at the scene, and an officer noted “significant evidence” was missing.

Police have not said whether Davies had a weapon near him at the scene.

name: Emmett Till
summary: Emmett Till, 14, of Chicago, was abducted from his great-uncle's home near Money, Mississippi, on August 28, 1955, and beaten, shot, and thrown into the Tallahatchie River after Carolyn Bryant, a white woman working at a local store, accused him of grabbing her and making sexual advances. Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam, her husband and brother-in-law, were tried for murder and acquitted by an all-white jury within about an hour; months later, protected by double jeopardy, they confessed to the killing in a paid magazine interview. Neither man was ever punished, and no one has ever been convicted in the case. Till's mother's decision to hold an open-casket funeral, and photographs of his mutilated body published in Jet magazine, helped galvanize the civil rights movement.
known: Till's abduction, the accusation by Carolyn Bryant, and the murder itself, per contemporaneous 1955 trial testimony and reporting.
Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam were tried for murder and acquitted by an all-white jury in September 1955, a verdict reached quickly.
Months after the acquittal, protected from further prosecution by double jeopardy, Bryant and Milam confessed to the killing in a paid interview with Look magazine.

The U.S. Department of Justice reopened the investigation twice (2004 and 2018) and closed it both times without new charges, most recently in December 2021, citing insufficient evidence to prove Carolyn Bryant Donham had lied to the FBI about a later-alleged recantation.

In 2022, Till family researchers discovered an unserved 1955 arrest warrant for Donham (then named as “Mrs. Roy Bryant”) in the Leflore County courthouse basement; a Leflore County grand jury heard the case that August and declined to indict her on kidnapping or manslaughter charges.
Bryant and Milam are both dead. Donham died in Louisiana on April 25, 2023, having never been charged in the case.
unknown: Whether Till in fact touched or spoke inappropriately to Bryant, or whether her account was accurate, has never been independently established — accounts from witnesses who were with Till that day differ from hers.
Bryant and Milam described the killing in their paid 1956 confession, but that account has never been tested by cross-examination or an actual conviction, and its full accuracy is unverified.

Whether Carolyn Bryant Donham identified Till to Bryant and Milam on the night of the abduction, as some witnesses alleged, versus attempting to intervene, as she claimed in a later unpublished memoir, was never resolved by the 2022 grand jury.
unanswered: Why was the 1955 arrest warrant for Donham never served, when police reportedly knew her location for at least part of the time?
What specifically did the 2022 Leflore County grand jury find insufficient in the evidence against Donham, given the additional decades of investigation and the since-discovered warrant?
Were there other participants in the abduction or killing beyond Bryant, Milam, and Donham who were never identified or charged?

name: Malcolm X
summary: Malcolm X, 39, was shot and killed while delivering a speech at the Audubon Ballroom in the Washington Heights neighborhood of Manhattan on February 21, 1965. Talmadge Hayer (also known as Mujahid Abdul Halim) was caught at the scene and confessed to being one of the shooters; he, along with Muhammad Aziz and Khalil Islam, were convicted of murder in 1966. Aziz and Islam always maintained their innocence, and in November 2021 a joint reinvestigation by the Manhattan District Attorney's office and the men's attorneys resulted in both convictions being vacated, citing withheld exculpatory evidence. Hayer had named four other men as participants in a 1978 affidavit, but that information was never used to reopen the case at the time, and no one beyond Hayer has ever been properly convicted of the killing.
known: The shooting and Hayer's capture and confession at the scene, per contemporaneous 1965 police and trial records.
Aziz, Islam, and Hayer were convicted of murder in 1966.

In a 1977–78 affidavit, Hayer stated that Aziz and Islam were not involved and separately named four other men he said helped plan and carry out the killing; a judge at the time declined to reopen the case on that basis, per the Innocence Project.

In November 2021, the Manhattan DA's office moved to vacate Aziz's and Islam's convictions after a reinvestigation found the FBI and NYPD had withheld evidence likely to have changed the trial's outcome; both men were exonerated, Islam posthumously.
New York City and State later paid Aziz and Islam's estate a combined $36 million in settlements over the wrongful convictions.
unknown: The identities of the men Hayer named in his 1978 affidavit beyond Hayer himself have never resulted in any prosecution.

Whether or how federal and city law enforcement's own conduct around the investigation — including withheld evidence cited in the 2021 reinvestigation — affected the outcome has not been fully accounted for publicly.
No one beyond Hayer has ever been properly convicted and had that conviction stand for the killing.
unanswered: Why was Hayer's 1978 affidavit naming other participants never used to reopen the investigation at the time?
What specific evidence did the FBI and NYPD withhold from the original 1966 trial, and why?
Will any of the men named in Hayer's affidavit ever face investigation or charges?

name: Fred Hampton
summary: Fred Hampton, 21, chairman of the Illinois chapter of the Black Panther Party, was shot and killed in his bed during a pre-dawn raid on his Chicago apartment on December 4, 1969, carried out by a tactical unit assembled by Cook County State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan in coordination with the FBI. Fellow Panther Mark Clark was also killed. A coroner's inquest initially ruled the deaths justifiable homicide, but a 13-year civil lawsuit brought by survivors and the victims' families produced evidence of FBI involvement, including an informant who supplied a floor plan of the apartment marking Hampton's bed. The case ended in a 1982 settlement, not a criminal conviction: no officer, agent, or official involved in the raid was ever criminally charged or convicted for the deaths.
known: The raid, the deaths of Hampton and Clark, and the initial “justifiable homicide” coroner's ruling, per contemporaneous 1969–70 records.

FBI informant William O'Neal, who had infiltrated the Chicago Black Panther Party, supplied federal agents a floor plan of the apartment that marked the location of Hampton's bed, per documents surfaced in the subsequent civil litigation and later congressional review.

The Church Committee's 1975 Senate investigation found the FBI's COINTELPRO program had used improper and, in the committee's words, dangerous tactics against domestic political organizations including the Black Panther Party.

In 1982, the City of Chicago, Cook County, and the federal government settled the survivors' and families' civil lawsuit for $1.85 million, split evenly three ways, without formally admitting wrongdoing; the plaintiffs' attorney called it an admission of a conspiracy between the FBI and Hanrahan's men.
No officer, agent, or official involved in the raid was ever criminally charged or convicted for the deaths of Hampton or Clark.
unknown: The full extent of the FBI's direct role in planning the raid, beyond the floor plan supplied by O'Neal, has never been fully accounted for in a criminal proceeding.
Independent autopsy findings showed a dangerous level of barbiturates in Hampton's bloodstream despite initial toxicology tests finding none; how that discrepancy arose has never been resolved.
Which individual officer fired the shots described by witnesses as killing Hampton at close range after he was already down has never been established in any criminal finding.

name: Amadou Diallo
summary: Amadou Diallo, 23, an unarmed immigrant from Guinea, was shot and killed just after midnight on February 4, 1999 outside his Bronx apartment building by four plainclothes NYPD Street Crime Unit officers, who fired 41 rounds, 19 of which struck him. The officers said they believed Diallo, who was reaching for his wallet, matched the description of a rape suspect and that they mistook the wallet for a gun. A Bronx grand jury indicted all four officers on second-degree murder and other charges; the trial was moved to Albany, and on February 25, 2000, the jury acquitted all four of every charge. The Department of Justice later found insufficient evidence to bring federal charges. No one has ever been held criminally responsible for Diallo's death.
known: The shooting, the 41 rounds fired, and the 19 that struck Diallo, per the Bronx grand jury indictment and trial record.

The four officers — Sean Carroll, Edward McMellon, Kenneth Boss, and Richard Murphy — were indicted on second-degree murder and other charges, tried in Albany after a change of venue, and acquitted of all charges on February 25, 2000.
The U.S. Department of Justice separately reviewed the case and found insufficient evidence to bring federal civil rights charges.
The city of New York settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Diallo's family for $3 million, without admitting liability.
The NYPD's Street Crime Unit, to which all four officers belonged, was disbanded in 2002 following the case.
unknown: Whether Diallo made any movement that could reasonably have been mistaken as reaching for a weapon, versus simply retrieving his wallet as he had been asked, was disputed at trial and never resolved beyond the acquittal.
Eyewitness Sherrie Elliott testified that officers continued firing after Diallo had already fallen; that account was not accepted by the jury as sufficient to convict.
No individual officer has ever been identified as bearing greater responsibility than the others for the number of rounds fired.
unanswered: Why did the jury — which included Black jurors — find the officers' account of mistaking a wallet for a gun sufficient to acquit on all charges, including lesser counts like reckless endangerment?
What specific evidence did the Department of Justice find insufficient for federal civil rights charges?
What became of each of the four officers' careers after the acquittal, and were any ever disciplined internally beyond retraining?

name: Sean Bell
summary: Sean Bell, 23, was shot and killed by NYPD undercover officers in Jamaica, Queens in the early morning hours of November 25, 2006 — the day he was to be married. Officers fired 50 rounds at Bell and his two friends, Trent Benefield and Joseph Guzman, as the men left Bell's bachelor party; no weapon was ever recovered from the vehicle. Detectives Gescard Isnora and Michael Oliver were charged with manslaughter and Detective Marc Cooper with reckless endangerment. In April 2008, a judge acquitted all three of every charge, ruling that prosecutors had not proven their actions were unjustified. Federal prosecutors declined to bring civil rights charges. No one has ever been held criminally responsible for Bell's death.

Justice Arthur Cooperman acquitted all three defendants of every charge on April 25, 2008, stating the prosecution had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the officers' actions were unjustified.
Federal prosecutors reviewed the case and declined to bring civil rights charges against any of the officers involved.
The city of New York settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Bell's family for $3.25 million.
unknown: Whether Bell's car in fact struck an officer (Isnora), as the defense argued, in a manner that justified the volume of gunfire that followed remains disputed — the judge found the officers' account more credible, but the prosecution's witnesses gave a different version.

What became of the disciplinary proceedings against the involved officers, delayed for years after the acquittal, has received limited public follow-up.

name: Trayvon Martin
summary: Trayvon Martin, 17, was shot and killed by George Zimmerman, a neighborhood watch volunteer, inside a gated community in Sanford, Florida on February 26, 2012. Martin was unarmed, walking back from a convenience store. Zimmerman, who had called police to report Martin as suspicious before following him, claimed he acted in self-defense during a physical altercation. Charges were filed only after weeks of public pressure; a jury acquitted Zimmerman of second-degree murder and manslaughter in July 2013. The U.S. Department of Justice separately investigated and did not bring federal civil rights charges. No one has ever been held criminally responsible for Martin's death.

Zimmerman was charged with second-degree murder more than six weeks after the shooting, following public pressure and the appointment of a special prosecutor.
An all-women jury acquitted Zimmerman of both second-degree murder and manslaughter on July 13, 2013, after roughly 16 hours of deliberation.
The U.S. Department of Justice investigated separately for potential federal civil rights violations and ultimately did not bring charges.

name: Freddie Gray
summary: Freddie Gray, 25, suffered a fatal spinal cord injury while in the back of a Baltimore Police transport van after his arrest on April 12, 2015, and died a week later. The city medical examiner ruled his death a homicide. Six officers were criminally charged, with counts ranging from misconduct in office to second-degree “depraved heart” murder. Four officers went to trial: three were acquitted by a judge and one trial ended in a hung jury. Prosecutors then dropped all remaining charges against the other officers in July 2016, securing no convictions. The U.S. Department of Justice separately reviewed the case and declined federal prosecution. No one has ever been convicted in Freddie Gray's death.
known: Gray's arrest, the injury sustained in the police van, and his death a week later, per the Baltimore Police Department and the state's attorney's charging documents.
The city medical examiner ruled the death a homicide.
Six officers — Caesar Goodson, William Porter, Garrett Miller, Edward Nero, Brian Rice, and Alicia White — were criminally charged in May 2015.
Of the four officers who went to trial, three (Nero, Goodson, and Rice) were acquitted by Judge Barry Williams in bench trials, and one (Porter) ended in a mistrial after a hung jury.
In July 2016, Baltimore State's Attorney Marilyn Mosby dropped all remaining charges against the other officers, stating she still believed the death was a homicide but could not secure a conviction.
The U.S. Department of Justice reviewed the case for federal civil rights charges and declined to prosecute, per its own public statement.
unknown: The specific point at which Gray's spinal injury occurred during transport, and which officer's actions or inaction caused it, was never established to a court's satisfaction in any of the trials.
Whether the failure to seatbelt Gray in the van, as prosecutors alleged, was department policy in practice versus a documented violation specific to these officers, was disputed at trial.
Full findings of the Montgomery County Police Department's internal administrative investigation, which recommended discipline for some officers, were not made fully public.
unanswered: Why was the prosecution unable to secure a conviction on any of the six officers despite the medical examiner's homicide ruling?
What specific evidence did the Department of Justice find insufficient for federal civil rights charges?
What ultimately came of the internal disciplinary findings against individual officers, several of whom continued or advanced their careers within the department afterward?

name: Breonna Taylor
summary: Breonna Taylor, 26, an emergency room technician, was shot and killed by Louisville Metro Police officers executing a no-knock search warrant at her apartment shortly after midnight on March 13, 2020. The warrant was later found to have been based on falsified information. Taylor's boyfriend, believing intruders had broken in, fired a shot that struck an officer; police returned more than 30 rounds, killing Taylor. A local grand jury declined to charge any officer for her death. The U.S. Department of Justice later brought federal civil rights charges against four current and former officers; only one, Brett Hankison, was convicted, for firing blindly into the apartment — not for killing Taylor, since his shots never struck her. No one has ever been charged with, or convicted of, causing Taylor's death itself.
known: The raid, the warrant, and Taylor's death, per Louisville Metro Police Department records and the subsequent federal investigation.

A Jefferson County grand jury in September 2020 declined to charge any officer with Taylor's death; one officer, Hankison, was indicted only on charges of endangering her neighbors, and was acquitted of those state charges at trial in 2022.
In 2022, the FBI arrested and the DOJ federally charged four current and former officers with civil rights violations connected to the raid and the falsified warrant.

Hankison was convicted by a federal jury in November 2024 on one count of violating Taylor's civil rights for firing 10 shots blindly through a covered window; the jury separately cleared him of a charge involving her neighbors.

The Department of Justice's own sentencing memo, filed under a later administration, stated Hankison “did not shoot Ms. Taylor and is not otherwise responsible for her death,” and recommended a one-day sentence; the judge sentenced him to roughly 33 months instead.
No officer has ever been charged with or convicted of causing Taylor's death.
unknown: Which specific officer's bullet caused Taylor's fatal wounds has never been the basis of any criminal charge.
The full extent of what individual officers knew about the falsified warrant application before the raid was disputed across the various proceedings.
The outcomes of the other federally charged officers' cases, including one whose state charges were dismissed by a federal judge in 2026, remain only partially resolved.
unanswered: Why did the local grand jury decline to charge any officer with Taylor's death itself, and what evidence was or was not presented to it?
Why has no officer ever been charged specifically with causing Taylor's death, as opposed to endangerment or civil rights violations connected to the raid?
What accounts for the DOJ's own shift in position on the case's severity between the prosecution that secured Hankison's conviction and the sentencing memo that followed?

name: Rekia Boyd
summary: Rekia Boyd, 22, was shot and killed by off-duty Chicago Police Detective Dante Servin near Douglas Park on the city's West Side in the early hours of March 21, 2012. Servin, in his car in a nearby alley, fired five shots over his shoulder at a group Boyd was part of, striking a man in the hand and Boyd in the back of the head; he said he believed one of the group had pulled a gun, but no weapon was ever found. Servin was charged nearly two years later with involuntary manslaughter and reckless discharge of a firearm. At his 2015 bench trial, the judge issued a directed verdict of not guilty before the defense even presented its case, ruling that Servin's conduct was intentional rather than reckless — meaning prosecutors had charged the wrong offense — while noting Servin's actions were “beyond reckless.” Because of double jeopardy, he could never be retried on a more serious charge. No one has ever been convicted in Boyd's death.
known: The shooting, the five shots fired, and Boyd's death, per Chicago Police Department records and subsequent trial testimony.
No weapon was ever recovered from the scene despite an extended police search, per contemporaneous reporting.
Servin was charged in January 2014 with involuntary manslaughter, reckless discharge of a firearm, and reckless conduct.

At an April 2015 bench trial, Cook County Judge Dennis Porter issued a directed finding of not guilty on all counts, ruling that the evidence showed Servin's firing was intentional rather than reckless — meaning it should have been charged as a more serious offense — and that the involuntary manslaughter charge as filed could not be sustained.

The judge stated Servin's conduct was “beyond reckless,” but because of the specific charge filed, was legally barred from convicting him of anything greater; double jeopardy protections mean Servin can never be retried on a murder charge for Boyd's death.
The city of Chicago settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Boyd's family for $4.5 million in 2013, before the criminal trial concluded.
In 2019, a different Cook County judge declined to expunge Servin's record, citing the strength of the evidence presented at trial despite the acquittal.
unknown: Whether a member of Boyd's group in fact possessed or displayed a weapon, as Servin claimed, was never resolved — no weapon was found, but the claim was never conclusively disproven in court either.

Why the Cook County State's Attorney's office originally filed involuntary manslaughter rather than a murder charge, given the judge's later finding that the conduct was intentional, has not been fully explained by prosecutors.
The full internal disciplinary history and departure circumstances for Servin from the Chicago Police Department following the case have not been comprehensively documented.
unanswered: Why did prosecutors choose to charge involuntary manslaughter rather than a charge that matched what the trial judge later found the evidence showed?
What accountability mechanisms, if any, exist for cases where a charging decision itself forecloses a conviction that the evidence might otherwise support?
What became of the group Boyd was with that night, and has any of them ever spoken publicly about what happened in the moments before the shooting?

name: Eric Garner
summary: Eric Garner, 43, died on July 17, 2014 after NYPD Officer Daniel Pantaleo placed him in an apparent chokehold — a maneuver banned under NYPD policy — while arresting him on suspicion of selling untaxed loose cigarettes on a Staten Island street corner. Bystander video captured Garner repeating “I can't breathe” eleven times before he lost consciousness. The city medical examiner ruled his death a homicide, citing the chokehold as a contributing cause. A Staten Island grand jury declined to indict Pantaleo in December 2014. The Department of Justice's five-year federal civil rights investigation ended in July 2019, one day before the fifth anniversary of Garner's death, with Attorney General William Barr declining to bring charges. Pantaleo was fired from the NYPD in an internal disciplinary proceeding later that year, but no criminal charge was ever filed against him or anyone else involved in Garner's death.
known: The arrest, the chokehold captured on bystander video, and Garner's death, per the New York City medical examiner's office and contemporaneous reporting.
The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide, finding the chokehold, along with compression of his chest and prone positioning during the arrest, contributed to his death.
A Staten Island grand jury, composed of 15 white and 8 minority jurors, declined to indict Pantaleo on any charge in December 2014.

In July 2019, the Department of Justice concluded a five-year federal civil rights investigation and declined to bring charges, a decision made personally by Attorney General William Barr following the recommendation of Brooklyn federal prosecutors.
An NYPD internal disciplinary trial in 2019 found Pantaleo had used a prohibited chokehold; he was fired from the department later that year — an administrative outcome, not a criminal one.
New York City settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Garner's family for $5.9 million in 2015.

name: Tamir Rice
summary: Tamir Rice, 12, was shot and killed by rookie Cleveland Police Officer Timothy Loehmann on November 22, 2014, within two seconds of Loehmann's patrol car skidding to a stop beside him outside a recreation center. Rice had been playing with a pellet gun; the 911 caller told the dispatcher the gun was “probably fake” and the person waving it was “probably a juvenile,” but that information was never relayed to the responding officers. A grand jury declined to indict Loehmann or his partner, Frank Garmback, in December 2015, with the county prosecutor calling the shooting a “perfect storm of human error” rather than a crime. The Department of Justice closed a five-year federal civil rights investigation in December 2020 without charges. No one has ever been criminally charged in Tamir Rice's death.

The 911 caller's qualifications — that the gun was probably fake and the person was probably a juvenile — were not relayed by the dispatcher to Loehmann and Garmback before they arrived, per the prosecutor's own account.
A Cuyahoga County grand jury declined to indict either officer on any charge in December 2015; prosecutor Timothy McGinty stated he had recommended against indictment.

The City of Cleveland fired Loehmann in 2017 — explicitly not for the shooting, but for omitting from his job application that a previous department had found him emotionally unfit for police work.

Loehmann was hired by at least two other police departments after his firing, each time resigning or withdrawing following public backlash led by Rice's mother, Samaria Rice.

The specific tactical decision to drive the patrol car directly up to Rice at close range, rather than approaching from a distance, was criticized by outside police-practice experts but was not the basis for any criminal charge.

Why were other police departments able to hire Loehmann in the years after his firing without his history in the Rice shooting surfacing during hiring review?

name: Philando Castile
summary: Philando Castile, 32, a St. Paul-area elementary school cafeteria supervisor, was shot and killed by St. Anthony Police Officer Jeronimo Yanez during a traffic stop in Falcon Heights, Minnesota on July 6, 2016. Castile, who had a permit to carry, calmly informed Yanez he had a firearm in the car; Yanez fired seven shots, striking him five times, as Castile's girlfriend Diamond Reynolds and her 4-year-old daughter sat in the car. Reynolds began livestreaming the aftermath on Facebook within moments, and the video was viewed by millions. Yanez was charged with second-degree manslaughter and two counts of endangering Reynolds and her daughter; a jury acquitted him of all charges on June 16, 2017, after roughly 27 hours of deliberation. No one has ever been convicted in Castile's death.

The City of St. Anthony announced it would dismiss Yanez from the police force the same day as the acquittal, offering him a voluntary separation rather than returning him to duty.
The City of St. Anthony and surrounding jurisdictions reached a $3 million settlement with Castile's family in 2017; St. Anthony also later disbanded its police department entirely.

name: Stephon Clark
summary: Stephon Clark, 22, was shot and killed by Sacramento Police officers Terrence Mercadal and Jared Robinet in his grandmother's backyard on March 18, 2018, after they responded to a report of vandalism and pursued him on foot. The officers said they believed Clark was pointing a gun at them in the dark; he was holding only a cellphone. Sacramento County District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert announced in March 2019 that no criminal charges would be filed. Days later, California Attorney General Xavier Becerra's independent state review reached the same conclusion. In September 2019, federal prosecutors also declined to bring civil rights charges. Three separate reviews — county, state, and federal — each concluded independently that no charges could be sustained, and no one has ever been convicted in Clark's death.

Federal prosecutors and the FBI announced on September 26, 2019 that they found insufficient evidence to support federal civil rights charges.

The shooting and subsequent non-charging decisions prompted sustained protests in Sacramento, and contributed to California signing a 2019 law raising the legal standard for police use of deadly force.

name: Michael Brown
summary: Michael Brown, 18, was shot and killed by Ferguson, Missouri Police Officer Darren Wilson on August 9, 2014, following a confrontation after Wilson stopped Brown and a friend for walking in the street. Brown's body remained in the street for roughly four hours afterward, which inflamed already-tense relations between the majority-Black city and its overwhelmingly white police force. A St. Louis County grand jury declined to indict Wilson in November 2014. The Department of Justice separately cleared Wilson of civil rights violations in March 2015, while issuing a scathing report finding Ferguson's police and courts had systematically targeted Black residents for revenue rather than public safety. In 2020, the county's first Black prosecutor, Wesley Bell, reopened the case at the family's request and, after a five-month independent review, announced in 2020 that he too could not prove murder or manslaughter charges. Three separate reviewing authorities have now each declined to charge Wilson, who resigned days after the grand jury decision; no one has ever been charged in Brown's death.
known: The August 9, 2014 shooting and the roughly four hours Brown's body remained on Canfield Drive afterward, per contemporaneous reporting and the DOJ's 2015 report.
A St. Louis County grand jury of nine white and three Black jurors declined to indict Wilson on November 24, 2014; Wilson resigned from the Ferguson Police Department days later.

The DOJ's March 2015 report cleared Wilson of federal civil rights violations, concluding prosecutors could not disprove his account that he feared for his life, while a companion DOJ report found a pattern of Ferguson police and courts systematically targeting Black residents for fines and fees.

In 2020, St. Louis County's first Black prosecuting attorney, Wesley Bell, reopened the case at the family's request; after a five-month independent review, he announced he could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Wilson committed murder or manslaughter under Missouri law.
Autopsy results cited in the DOJ report found Brown was struck six to eight times.
unknown: Whether Brown had his hands raised in surrender, as some witnesses said, or was moving toward Wilson, as Wilson testified and the DOJ report found more consistent with physical evidence, was never resolved in any court proceeding.
The full physical struggle at Wilson's vehicle, including whether Brown reached inside it, was reconstructed from disputed witness accounts rather than settled by any trial.

name: Alton Sterling
summary: Alton Sterling, 37, a father of five who sold homemade CDs outside a Baton Rouge convenience store, was shot and killed by Officers Blane Salamoni and Howie Lake II on July 5, 2016, during a struggle after the two officers responded to a report of a man threatening someone with a gun. Cellphone video of the roughly 90-second encounter, showing Sterling pinned to the ground when he was shot, circulated widely and prompted nationwide protests. The Department of Justice declined to bring federal civil rights charges in May 2017. Nearly a year later, in March 2018, Louisiana's attorney general separately declined to bring state charges, calling the shooting “justifiable” and citing a toxicology report showing Sterling had drugs in his system. No one has ever been criminally charged in Sterling's death.
known: The struggle, the shooting, and Sterling's death outside the Triple S Food Mart, per cellphone video and the subsequent DOJ and state investigations.

Louisiana Attorney General Jeff Landry announced in March 2018, after reviewing the DOJ's evidence and conducting independent interviews, that his office would not bring state charges either, calling the officers' actions “justifiable.”

East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore recused his own office from the state review due to a professional relationship with one officer's parents, leaving the decision to the state attorney general.
Sterling's family filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the city, its police department, and the two officers in June 2017.

name: John Crawford III
summary: John Crawford III, 22, was shot and killed by Beavercreek, Ohio Police Officer Sean Williams inside a Walmart store on August 5, 2014, while talking on his cell phone and holding an unboxed BB/pellet air rifle he had picked up from a store shelf. A 911 caller, Ronald Ritchie, had told dispatchers a man was waving a gun at customers — an account store surveillance video later contradicted, showing Crawford never pointed the item at anyone. A special Greene County grand jury declined to indict Williams in September 2014, the same day the Department of Justice opened its own civil rights investigation; that federal review closed in July 2017 without charges, finding insufficient evidence that Williams had willfully violated Crawford's civil rights. No one has ever been charged in Crawford's death.
known: The 911 call reporting a man with a gun, the shooting, and Crawford's death, per Walmart surveillance footage and the 911 audio, both later released publicly.
Surveillance video showed Crawford was not pointing the air rifle at anyone and was largely engaged in a phone call in the moments before he was shot, contradicting the 911 caller's account.
A special Greene County grand jury of nine members declined to indict Officer Williams on September 24, 2014; special prosecutor Mark Piepmeier stated Crawford “did nothing wrong.”

The Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division and the U.S. Attorney's Office for Southern Ohio announced on July 11, 2017 that evidence was insufficient to prove Williams had willfully violated Crawford's federal civil rights.
A separate investigation concluded the 911 caller, Ronald Ritchie, would not be charged for his report, as prosecutors found no evidence he knowingly provided false information.
unknown: Whether Officer Williams had a reasonable opportunity to perceive that Crawford was not an active threat before firing, given the surveillance video's contradiction of the initial 911 report, was never tested at trial.

The precise verbal commands given to Crawford immediately before the shooting, and how much time he had to respond to them, were disputed between the family's account and the responding officers' statements.
Whether internal Beavercreek Police Department training or policy changed as a direct result of the shooting has not been comprehensively documented in public reporting.
unanswered: Why did the grand jury's and DOJ's conclusions differ so sharply from the family attorney's assessment that the surveillance video showed “ample evidence” for charges?
What became of the Crawford family's separate civil lawsuit against Walmart and the Beavercreek Police Department?
Why was a 911 caller whose account was directly contradicted by video evidence not held to any legal accountability for that report?

NPR — “Grand Jury Won't Indict Officers In Ohio Wal-Mart Shooting”

name: Sandra Bland
summary: Sandra Bland, 28, was found dead in her cell at the Waller County Jail in Hempstead, Texas on July 13, 2015, three days after Texas State Trooper Brian Encinia arrested her during a traffic stop in nearby Prairie View for failing to signal a lane change. Dashcam video showed the stop escalating after Bland questioned why she had to put out her cigarette, ending with Encinia drawing a Taser and pulling her from her car. Her death was ruled a suicide by asphyxiation. A Waller County grand jury found no criminal wrongdoing by jailers or the sheriff's office, but did indict Encinia on a misdemeanor perjury charge for falsely writing that he removed Bland from her car to conduct a “safer traffic investigation.” That charge — the only criminal charge ever filed against anyone in connection with Bland's death — was dropped in June 2017 after Encinia agreed to surrender his peace officer license and never work in law enforcement again. No one has ever been convicted of any crime related to Bland's arrest, treatment, or death.
known: The traffic stop, its escalation, and the circumstances of the arrest, per Texas Department of Public Safety dashcam footage and a cell phone video Bland recorded herself.
Bland was found dead in her cell three days later; the Harris County Medical Examiner ruled the death a suicide by asphyxiation using a plastic garbage bag.

A Waller County grand jury found no felony had been committed by jailers or the sheriff's office, but indicted Encinia in January 2016 on a single misdemeanor perjury charge for his written account of the arrest.
Encinia was fired by the Texas Department of Public Safety in March 2016 following the indictment.

In June 2017, the sole perjury charge against Encinia was dismissed at prosecutors' request after he agreed to permanently surrender his peace officer license, never work in law enforcement again, and never seek to have the charge expunged.
Bland's family settled a wrongful death lawsuit against Waller County and the Texas Department of Public Safety for $1.9 million in September 2016.

The Texas Legislature passed the Sandra Bland Act in 2017, mandating that county jails divert people with mental health or substance abuse issues toward treatment and requiring independent investigation of jail deaths — though the bill was significantly narrowed from its original scope during the legislative process.
unknown: Whether Bland's death was in fact a suicide, as officially ruled, continues to be disputed by her family and some outside observers, though no official investigation has overturned the medical examiner's finding.

Whether jail staff followed required cell-check protocols in the hours before Bland's death was examined by the grand jury, which found no felony conduct, but the full internal findings were not comprehensively made public.

Whether Encinia's conduct during the arrest itself, beyond the specific written misstatement charged as perjury, was ever independently assessed for criminal liability separate from the dropped charge.
unanswered: Why was perjury — a charge about a written statement made after the arrest — the only charge ever brought, when video showed Encinia drawing a weapon and pulling Bland from her vehicle during a stop for a minor traffic violation?
What jail protocols, if any, were not followed in the three days between Bland's arrest and her death, and were any jail employees ever held accountable?
How much of the original, broader version of the Sandra Bland Act — which initially included stronger police accountability provisions — was ultimately removed before passage, and why?

The Texas Tribune — “Perjury charge dropped against trooper who arrested Sandra Bland”

name: Terence Crutcher
summary: Terence Crutcher, 40, was shot and killed by Tulsa Police Officer Betty Shelby on September 16, 2016, after she encountered him beside his stalled SUV in the middle of a north Tulsa street. Video from a police helicopter piloted by Shelby's own husband and from officers' body cameras showed Crutcher walking toward his vehicle with his hands visible before Shelby fired; the helicopter pilot could be heard remarking that Crutcher “looks like a bad dude.” Shelby testified she believed Crutcher was reaching into the vehicle for a weapon; no weapon was found. She was charged with first-degree manslaughter and, after nine hours of jury deliberation, acquitted of all charges on May 17, 2017. Crutcher's family called the verdict an injustice; no one has ever been convicted in his death.
known: The encounter, the shooting, and Crutcher's death, per body camera and police helicopter video that was released publicly.
No weapon was recovered from Crutcher's vehicle or person.
Tulsa County District Attorney Steve Kunzweiler charged Shelby with first-degree manslaughter less than a week after the shooting.
A 12-member jury, including three Black jurors, deliberated for nine hours before acquitting Shelby of all charges on May 17, 2017; several jurors were reported crying as the verdict was read.
Shelby was reinstated to the Tulsa Police Department in an administrative role following her acquittal, then resigned from the department in August 2017.
An autopsy found PCP in Crutcher's system at the time of the shooting, which the defense raised at trial; the family's attorneys argued this did not justify the shooting regardless.
unknown: Whether Crutcher was in fact reaching into his vehicle, as Shelby testified, versus simply attempting to comply or retrieve documentation, was disputed by the family's attorneys based on the same video evidence and never resolved beyond the acquittal.
The full content and reasoning behind the jury's nine hours of deliberation is not public, as with all jury deliberations.
Whether the Department of Justice's separate federal civil rights review, opened after the state acquittal, reached a final public conclusion has not been consistently reported in available sources.
unanswered: Why did the jury find Shelby's account of reaching for a weapon credible when body camera video reviewed by outside experts showed Crutcher's hands were not near the vehicle's interior at the moment of the shooting?
What became of the Department of Justice's civil rights investigation into the shooting, opened following Shelby's state acquittal?
What internal Tulsa Police Department policy changes, if any, resulted directly from this case regarding response to stalled-vehicle calls?

name: Samuel DuBose
summary: Samuel DuBose, 43, was shot in the head and killed by University of Cincinnati Police Officer Ray Tensing during a traffic stop on July 19, 2015, after Tensing pulled him over for a missing front license plate. Body camera video showed a brief exchange over DuBose's license before he began to drive away; Tensing testified he was dragged by the car and feared for his life, while the county prosecutor called the shooting “asinine” and “totally unwarranted” when announcing a murder indictment less than two weeks later. Two separate juries, in trials roughly eight months apart, deadlocked and produced mistrials in 2016 and 2017. Hamilton County's prosecutor then dropped the case rather than pursue a third trial, saying jurors had told him he would never get twelve people to agree to convict a police officer. No one has ever been convicted in DuBose's death.
known: The traffic stop, the brief struggle, and the shooting, captured on Tensing's body camera and released publicly.
Hamilton County Prosecutor Joe Deters indicted Tensing on a murder charge less than two weeks after the shooting, calling his actions “asinine” and “totally unwarranted.”

A first jury deadlocked after roughly 25 hours of deliberation in November 2016, resulting in a mistrial; prosecutors said that jury had a majority favoring conviction on the lesser voluntary manslaughter charge.
A second jury deadlocked again after roughly 31 hours of deliberation in June 2017, resulting in a second mistrial.

In July 2017, Prosecutor Deters formally dropped the murder and voluntary manslaughter charges rather than pursue a third trial; the judge dismissed the case in a manner that permanently barred retrial on those charges, while declining the defense's request to formally acquit Tensing.

The University of Cincinnati settled a wrongful death lawsuit with DuBose's family for $4.85 million and a tuition-free college scholarship for his children in 2015, and separately disbanded its own police force's traffic-stop authority off campus.
unknown: Whether Tensing was in fact dragged by DuBose's car and reasonably feared for his life, as he testified, or whether the body camera video showed a shooting that occurred before any such danger existed, as prosecutors argued, was never resolved — two separate juries considered the same video and could not agree.
The specific numerical breakdown of each deadlocked jury's votes was reported by prosecutors as favoring conviction after the first trial, but the precise count was not made formally public.
Whether federal civil rights charges, which the U.S. Attorney's office said it would consider after the state case ended, were ever formally pursued was not confirmed in available public reporting.
unanswered: Why did two separate juries, reviewing the same body camera footage, each fail to reach a unanimous verdict?
Did the U.S. Attorney's Office ultimately pursue or decline federal civil rights charges against Tensing after the state case was dismissed?
What specific reforms did the University of Cincinnati Police Department make to its traffic-stop authority and training as a result of this case?

name: Keith Lamont Scott
summary: Keith Lamont Scott, 43, a father of seven, was shot and killed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Officer Brentley Vinson on September 20, 2016, in an apartment complex parking lot. Officers were at the complex to serve a warrant on someone else when they encountered Scott, who has a brain injury, sitting in his SUV; police said body-camera video showed a gun in his hand as he exited the vehicle after repeated orders to drop it, while Scott's wife, who recorded the aftermath on her phone, said he had no gun and was unarmed. A firearm was recovered at the scene with Scott's fingerprints and DNA. After a two-month investigation, Mecklenburg County District Attorney Andrew Murray announced in November 2016 that Vinson — who is also Black — had acted lawfully, a conclusion 15 prosecutors in his office reached unanimously. No charges were ever filed against Vinson or any other officer at the scene.
known: The encounter, the shooting, and Scott's death, per police dashcam, body-worn camera, and his wife's cell phone video, all released publicly.
A handgun, reported stolen out of Gaston County, was recovered at the scene bearing Scott's fingerprints and DNA.

District Attorney Andrew Murray announced on November 30, 2016 that his office, after unanimous agreement among 15 prosecutors, would not charge Vinson, concluding the shooting was justified based on the totality of the evidence.
The North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Department of Justice both separately investigated the shooting alongside the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department's own review.
Scott's family filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the city and Vinson, alleging officers needlessly escalated an unconfirmed marijuana-possession stop into a fatal confrontation.
unknown: Whether Scott in fact held the recovered handgun in his hand at the moment he was shot, as police maintained body-camera video showed, or whether he was unarmed and reading a book, as his wife stated, was never resolved by any criminal proceeding since none occurred.

The family's lawsuit alleged Scott never raised his arms or made any threatening gesture; how this account squares with the DA's conclusion that the shooting was justified was not resolved through litigation before any reported settlement.

Whether Scott's brain injury, which his family said affected his ability to communicate and comply with commands, was factored into the DA's justification analysis was not detailed in the office's public statements.
unanswered: Why did the district attorney's office conclude the shooting was justified when the victim's own family disputed the central factual claim — that Scott was holding a weapon — underlying that conclusion?
What became of the wrongful death lawsuit Scott's family filed against the city and Officer Vinson?
What findings, if any, did the separate North Carolina SBI and DOJ investigations reach, beyond the county DA's own conclusion?

name: Ezell Ford
summary: Ezell Ford, 25, who his family said had a serious mental illness, was shot and killed by LAPD Officers Sharlton Wampler and Antonio Villegas on August 11, 2014, during a struggle after the officers stopped him while he was walking near his South Los Angeles home. Police said Ford grabbed for Wampler's holstered weapon during the struggle; DNA evidence supported that he was on top of Wampler at the time of the shooting. The Los Angeles Police Commission ruled in June 2015 that Wampler had no legal justification to stop Ford in the first place, making the entire encounter — and by extension the shooting — out of department policy. Despite that finding, the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office announced in January 2017, more than two years after the shooting, that neither officer would face criminal charges, concluding both had acted in lawful self-defense. No officer in Los Angeles County had been criminally charged for an on-duty shooting since 2000, and none was in Ford's case either.
known: The stop, struggle, and shooting, per the LAPD's own investigation and the district attorney's 28-page charging decision report.
DNA evidence indicated Ford was on top of Officer Wampler and struggling for his holstered weapon at the time of the shooting, per the DA's report.

The Los Angeles Police Commission ruled in June 2015 that Wampler had no legal basis to stop and pursue Ford, making the stop itself a violation of department policy, and that this violation extended to the use of deadly force that followed; the commission found Villegas's conduct largely within policy, apart from how he drew his weapon.

The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office announced on January 24, 2017 that both officers acted lawfully in self-defense and would not be charged, a decision reached despite the Police Commission's contrary policy finding.
The Los Angeles City Council approved a $1.5 million settlement with Ford's family in February 2017, weeks after the DA's decision.
Per a 2015 analysis, no Los Angeles County law enforcement officer had faced criminal charges for an on-duty shooting since 2000.
unknown: How the DA's office reconciled its self-defense finding with the Police Commission's separate, contrary conclusion that the underlying stop — and by extension the encounter that led to the shooting — violated department policy has not been fully explained publicly.
Whether officers were aware of, or had reason to know of, Ford's mental illness at the time they initiated the stop was disputed between the family's account and the department's official record.

What internal discipline, if any, either officer faced as a result of the Police Commission's out-of-policy finding, separate from the criminal charging decision, was not comprehensively documented in public reporting.
unanswered: Why did the district attorney's office reach a different conclusion than the city's own police oversight board on whether the underlying stop and shooting were justified?
Why did the criminal investigation take more than two years to conclude?

What accounts for the broader pattern the ACLU of Southern California identified — only one Southern California officer criminally charged for an on-duty shooting since 2000 — and has that pattern changed since?

name: Danroy Henry Jr.
summary: Danroy “DJ” Henry Jr., 20, a Pace University football player, was shot and killed by Pleasantville, New York Police Officer Aaron Hess on October 17, 2010, in a shopping center parking lot after officers responded to a bar disturbance following Pace's homecoming game. Henry was driving away in his car when Hess, on foot, ended up on the hood of the vehicle and fired through the windshield, saying he feared for his life; Henry's family disputed that account, saying Hess ran into the car's path. A Westchester County grand jury found no reasonable cause for an indictment in March 2011. The U.S. Department of Justice separately investigated and announced in 2015 that it would bring no federal civil rights charges. In 2023, more than a decade later, Westchester's District Attorney's office reopened the case as part of an independent review and again concluded there was no legal basis to prosecute. No one has ever been charged in Henry's death.
known: The shooting and Henry's death in the Thornwood shopping center parking lot, per Westchester County and federal investigation records.
Officer Aaron Hess acknowledged through his attorney that he fired the shots that killed Henry, stating he was on the hood of Henry's moving car and feared for his life.
A second officer, Ronald Beckley of the Mount Pleasant police, also fired at the vehicle, apparently striking the hood.
A Westchester County grand jury found no reasonable cause for an indictment in March 2011, under then-District Attorney Janet DiFiore.
U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara announced in 2015 that the evidence did not meet the exacting standard of criminal intent required for federal civil rights charges, following the DOJ's own investigation.

In 2023, Westchester District Attorney Miriam Rocah's office conducted an independent review of past police-involved deaths, including Henry's, and again concluded there was no legal basis to bring the case to a new grand jury.
Henry's family filed a $120 million federal lawsuit against the towns of Mount Pleasant and Pleasantville.
unknown: Whether Henry's car in fact struck Officer Hess before he fired, as Hess's attorney stated and prosecutors found credible, or whether Hess moved into the car's path, as the family's attorney alleged, was never resolved at trial since no charges were ever filed.
Witness accounts of the sequence of events differed sharply and were never reconciled through any adversarial court proceeding.
The specific new evidence or analysis, if any, that Westchester's 2023 independent review considered beyond the original 2011 and 2015 findings has not been made fully public.
unanswered: Why did three separate reviewing authorities — a county grand jury, the DOJ, and a reform-era DA's independent re-investigation over a decade later — each reach the same no-charges conclusion despite the family's persistent and specific factual dispute?
What became of the Henry family's $120 million federal lawsuit against Mount Pleasant and Pleasantville?

What prompted Westchester's DA to select Henry's case, alongside Kenneth Chamberlain Sr.'s, for independent re-review in 2023, and what criteria determine which past cases receive that kind of second look?

name: Kenneth Chamberlain Sr.
summary: Kenneth Chamberlain Sr., 68, a retired Marine and 20-year Westchester County corrections officer with a chronic heart condition, was shot and killed in his own White Plains apartment on November 19, 2011, after his medical alert pendant was triggered accidentally. Chamberlain repeatedly told police through the door that he did not need help and asked them to leave; after roughly an hour, officers broke the door down, used a Taser and beanbag rounds, and then fatally shot him. A Westchester County grand jury declined to indict any officer in May 2012. The Department of Justice's Southern District of New York investigated separately and closed its inquiry in 2017 without federal charges, and a federal civil jury cleared the city and the officer of liability in 2016. No one has ever been criminally charged in Chamberlain's death.
known: The medical alert trigger, the hour-long standoff, and the shooting, per police dashcam, stun-gun camera footage, and the medical alert company's recorded audio, later released publicly.
A Westchester County grand jury found no reasonable cause for an indictment against any officer in May 2012, per then-District Attorney Janet DiFiore.

Then-Westchester Public Safety Commissioner David Chong confirmed that one officer at the scene, Steven Hart, used a racial slur while outside Chamberlain's apartment, which the department said it would review.
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York closed its own federal civil rights investigation in 2017, finding insufficient evidence for prosecution.
A federal civil jury concluded in November 2016 that the City of White Plains and the officer who shot Chamberlain were not liable for his death, in a lawsuit brought by his family.
The City of White Plains separately agreed in 2023 to a $5 million settlement with Chamberlain's family — the largest in the city's history — resolving remaining civil claims.
unknown: Whether Chamberlain in fact brandished a knife at officers as they entered, as police maintained, was disputed by the family's attorney, who noted the only witnesses to that specific moment were the officers themselves.
The full content of the medical alert company's recorded audio from inside the apartment has not been comprehensively released to the public.
What specific review or discipline, if any, Officer Hart faced for the racial slur identified by the public safety commissioner has not been made public.
unanswered: Why did police continue and escalate a forced entry after being told repeatedly, over roughly an hour, that no medical emergency existed?
What became of the department's stated review of Officer Hart's use of a racial slur during the standoff?

Why did three separate proceedings — a grand jury, a federal civil rights investigation, and a federal civil trial — each conclude no one was liable, given the recorded evidence of Chamberlain's repeated statements that he needed no help?
