name: Jonathan Ferrell
summary: Jonathan Ferrell, 24, a former Florida A&M football player, was shot and killed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Officer Randall “Wes” Kerrick on September 14, 2013, after crawling from a wrecked car and banging on a nearby house's door seeking help; the resident, mistaking him for a home invader, called 911. Kerrick fired 12 rounds, striking Ferrell 10 times, eight while he was already on the ground; the two other responding officers did not fire. Kerrick was charged with voluntary manslaughter — the first Charlotte officer ever charged for an on-duty shooting — but a 2015 jury deadlocked 8-4 in favor of acquittal after four days of deliberation, resulting in a mistrial. North Carolina's attorney general declined to seek a retrial, and the charge was formally dismissed. No one has ever been convicted in Ferrell's death.
known: The car accident, Ferrell's approach to the house, and the shooting, per police dashcam footage and trial testimony.
Kerrick fired 12 shots, striking Ferrell 10 times; the two other officers at the scene did not fire their weapons.
Kerrick was arrested and charged with voluntary manslaughter within about 18 hours of the shooting, becoming the first Charlotte-Mecklenburg officer charged for an on-duty shooting.
A jury of eight women and four men deliberated for four days before deadlocking 8-4 in favor of acquittal; Judge Robert C. Ervin declared a mistrial on August 21, 2015.

North Carolina Attorney General Roy Cooper's office announced on August 28, 2015 that it would not seek a retrial, concluding a second trial was unlikely to yield a different result; the charge was dismissed.
Kerrick resigned from the department and reached a separation agreement including approximately $180,000 in back pay.
unknown: Whether Ferrell was charging at Kerrick, as Kerrick testified, or approaching in a manner that did not require deadly force, as prosecutors argued, was never resolved — the jury itself could not agree.
Why the two other officers on scene, facing the same situation, did not fire their weapons was raised by prosecutors at trial but not resolved as a formal finding.
The specific reasoning of the four jurors who favored conviction, versus the eight who favored acquittal, is not public, as with all jury deliberations.
unanswered: Why did a jury split so evenly on whether deadly force was justified when two of three responding officers did not fire?
What specific factors led North Carolina's attorney general to conclude a retrial would not yield a different outcome?
What, if any, use-of-force policy changes did the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department make as a direct result of this case?

name: Milton Hall
summary: Milton Hall, 49, a homeless man with a documented history of mental illness, was shot and killed by six Saginaw, Michigan police officers on July 1, 2012, in a parking lot after a dispute with a convenience store clerk. Eight officers formed a semicircle around Hall, who held a small pocketknife; after a police dog was allowed to bark and snap at him, six officers opened fire, striking him 11 times out of 46 rounds fired, continuing to shoot after he had collapsed. The Saginaw County prosecutor and the Michigan Attorney General's office both declined to bring criminal charges, finding the officers had not acted with criminal intent. The Department of Justice opened its own civil rights investigation and announced in February 2014 that it too would not prosecute, citing insufficient evidence of willful misconduct. No one has ever been charged in Hall's death.
known: The confrontation, the police dog, and the shooting of 46 rounds by six of eight officers present, striking Hall 11 times, per Saginaw County Prosecutor Mike Thomas's public account and video obtained by CNN.
The entire incident was captured on police dashcam video and a bystander's cellphone video, both later made public.

After a 10-week investigation, the Saginaw County prosecutor announced in September 2012 that the six officers who fired would not face criminal charges, concluding they had not acted with criminal intent.

The Saginaw Police Department demoted the on-site supervising officer to patrolman and disciplined two others for policy violations connected to the shooting; the six officers who fired remained on the force.

The U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Michigan, and the FBI jointly announced in February 2014 that the evidence was insufficient to prove the officers had willfully shot Hall for an unlawful purpose, and declined federal prosecution.
The ACLU of Michigan presented the case, including previously unreleased dashcam footage, to the Organization of American States' Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in October 2014.
unknown: Whether Hall's movements with the pocketknife, at the distance officers maintained, presented the imminent threat officers described has been disputed by the ACLU of Michigan and outside observers reviewing the same video the prosecutor's office relied on.
The specific individual conduct of each of the six officers who fired, versus the two who did not, has not been distinguished in public reporting beyond the aggregate shot count.
The precise nature of the internal discipline given to the supervising officer and two others, beyond a demotion, was not detailed publicly.
unanswered: Why did six armed officers, having already deployed a police dog and formed a wide perimeter, conclude that a barrage of 46 rounds was the only available response to a man holding a small pocketknife at a distance?
What specific evidence did both the county prosecutor's office and the Department of Justice find insufficient to establish criminal intent, given that video captured the entire incident?
What became of the six officers who fired and remained on the Saginaw police force after the shooting?

name: Miriam Carey
summary: Miriam Carey, 34, a dental hygienist from Stamford, Connecticut, was shot and killed by U.S. Secret Service and Capitol Police officers on October 3, 2013, after a seven-minute car chase that began when she drove into a restricted checkpoint near the White House with her 1-year-old daughter in the car and ended near the U.S. Capitol. Carey, who her family said had been hospitalized for postpartum depression, was unarmed; two officers each fired nine rounds in the final confrontation, striking her five times. Her daughter was found unharmed in the car. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia announced in July 2014 that it found insufficient evidence to bring federal civil rights or local charges against any officer involved. No one has ever been charged in Carey's death.
known: The White House checkpoint breach, the seven-minute chase to the Capitol, and the shooting, per the U.S. Attorney's Office's public account based on more than 60 witness interviews and physical evidence.
Carey was unarmed and not under the influence of drugs or alcohol, per the investigation; her 1-year-old daughter, in the car throughout, was found unharmed.
Two officers, one from the Secret Service and one from Capitol Police, each fired nine rounds in the final confrontation near the Capitol, striking Carey five times.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia announced on July 10, 2014 that there was insufficient evidence to prove the officers used excessive force or possessed criminal intent, and declined to bring any charges.
Carey's sister filed a $75 million wrongful death lawsuit against the Secret Service and Capitol Police, alleging a failure of firearms control among officers on scene.
unknown: Whether officers could have used other, less lethal means to stop Carey's vehicle before resorting to gunfire was raised publicly by observers and the family's attorney but was not addressed as a specific finding in the U.S. Attorney's public account.
The full internal review of the specific decision-making by the individual officers who fired, beyond the aggregate 18 rounds described publicly, has not been released.
The extent to which Carey's documented mental health history factored into how officers assessed and responded to the situation in real time was not detailed in the public charging decision.
unanswered: Why did officers at three separate locations over seven minutes escalate to lethal force against an unarmed woman with a child in the car, rather than attempting to disable the vehicle by other means?
What became of the Carey family's $75 million wrongful death lawsuit against the Secret Service and Capitol Police?
What specific evidence did the U.S. Attorney's Office weigh in concluding the officers' use of force did not meet the threshold for criminal intent?

name: Daniel Prude
summary: Daniel Prude, 41, a father of five visiting Rochester, New York from Chicago, died on March 30, 2020, a week after Rochester police officers restrained him naked on a snow-covered street during a mental health crisis. Body-camera video, not made public until September 2020, showed officers placing a mesh “spit hood” over his head and pressing his face into the pavement for roughly two minutes until he stopped breathing. The Monroe County medical examiner ruled his death a homicide from “complications of asphyxia in the setting of physical restraint.” New York Attorney General Letitia James's office presented the case to a grand jury, which voted 15–5 in February 2021 not to indict any of the three officers involved. No one has ever been charged in Prude's death.
known: The restraint, the spit hood, and Prude's death a week later, per body-camera video released by the family's attorneys in September 2020 and the Monroe County Medical Examiner's autopsy report.
The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide, citing asphyxia from physical restraint, with PCP listed as a contributing factor.
New York Attorney General Letitia James's office, required by state law to investigate police-involved deaths of unarmed civilians, presented a criminally negligent homicide charge to a grand jury.
The grand jury voted 15–5 not to indict any of the three officers, according to grand jury transcripts later released; five jurors indicated they would have voted to indict at least one officer.
Rochester's police chief was fired and seven officers were suspended in the aftermath of the video's public release, before the grand jury's decision.
The City of Rochester agreed to a $12 million settlement with Prude's estate for his five children in 2020.
unknown: Whether the specific restraint technique used — which a 2015 department training bulletin itself warned could cause fatal positional asphyxia — was applied in a manner consistent with that training was presented to the grand jury but not resolved by any indictment.

The full grand jury proceedings remain sealed by law beyond the vote count and portions of transcripts later released; the specific legal theory prosecutors argued for and against indictment on each officer individually is not fully public.

Internal emails later showed Rochester police commanders urged withholding the video's public release, citing fears of unrest; the full extent of who in city government was aware of this recommendation, and when, has not been comprehensively detailed.
unanswered: Why did five of twenty grand jurors favor indicting at least one officer while the majority did not, given a 2015 department training bulletin warning explicitly about the restraint position's asphyxiation risk?
What specific role did the delayed public release of the body-camera footage — nearly six months after Prude's death — play in the investigation and prosecution timeline?
What accountability, if any, did Rochester city officials face for the internal recommendation to delay releasing the video?

name: Manuel Ellis
summary: Manuel “Manny” Ellis, 33, died in a south Tacoma, Washington intersection on March 3, 2020, after Tacoma police officers tackled, punched, shocked him with a Taser, and restrained him face-down while he repeatedly told them he could not breathe. The Pierce County medical examiner ruled his death a homicide caused by oxygen deprivation from physical restraint. Washington's attorney general charged three officers in 2021 — the first time the state's AG had criminally charged officers for unlawful use of deadly force, using a new voter-approved police accountability law. After a nine-week trial, a Pierce County jury acquitted all three officers of every charge on December 21, 2023. The officers each subsequently received $500,000 to voluntarily leave the department. No one has ever been convicted in Ellis's death.
known: The confrontation, restraint, and Ellis's death, captured partly on a bystander's video, a doorbell camera, and police dispatch audio in which Ellis is heard repeatedly saying he could not breathe.
The Pierce County medical examiner ruled the death a homicide caused by oxygen deprivation from physical restraint.

Washington Attorney General Bob Ferguson charged officers Matthew Collins and Christopher Burbank with second-degree murder and manslaughter, and Officer Timothy Rankine with manslaughter, in May 2021.
A Pierce County jury acquitted all three officers of every charge on December 21, 2023, after a trial described as the largest single trial against law enforcement for an in-custody death since 1938.
Defense attorneys argued at trial that methamphetamine intoxication and a heart condition, not the officers' restraint, caused Ellis's death.

Following the acquittal, the Tacoma Police Department found none of the three officers had violated the department's use-of-force policy in effect at the time; all three subsequently received $500,000 separation payments to leave the department.
unknown: Whether the combination of restraint techniques and Ellis's underlying physical state was the actual mechanism of death, as the defense argued, or whether the restraint itself was the primary cause, as the medical examiner's ruling and prosecution argued, was contested by expert witnesses on both sides and not resolved beyond the acquittal.

The specific sequence of the initial contact — including what exactly officers observed before deciding to pursue and restrain Ellis — was disputed between witness accounts and the officers' testimony.
The jury's specific reasoning for acquitting on every charge, across three different defendants and multiple counts, is not public, as with all jury deliberations.
unanswered: Why did the first criminal trial of police officers under Washington's new voter-approved accountability law end in a full acquittal despite video and audio evidence of Ellis repeatedly saying he could not breathe?
What does the department's post-acquittal finding that no use-of-force policy was violated suggest about whether that policy itself needs to change?
What became of the Ellis family's pending federal civil rights lawsuit against the city of Tacoma, referenced during the criminal trial?

name: Relisha Rudd
summary: Relisha Rudd, 8, disappeared from Washington, D.C.'s D.C. General Family Shelter, where she lived with her mother and siblings, in early 2014. She was last seen on security footage on March 1, 2014, at a Northeast D.C. hotel with Kahlil Tatum, a 51-year-old shelter janitor with a prior felony record whom her mother had allowed to take her overnight. Her absence from school went unreported for roughly 18 days until a school counselor raised the alarm. Tatum was later found to have shot and killed his wife before being found dead of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound on April 1, 2014. Investigators believe Tatum killed Relisha before taking his own life, though her body has never been found and no charges have ever been filed in connection with her disappearance. Her case remains open more than a decade later.
known: Relisha's identity, age, and the March 1, 2014 sighting with Kahlil Tatum at a Northeast D.C. hotel, per the Metropolitan Police Department's official case listing and FBI surveillance footage.

Tatum, the shelter's janitor, had a prior felony record for burglary, larceny, and breaking-and-entering, and had befriended Relisha's mother, buying gifts and taking the family on outings before being allowed to take Relisha overnight.

Tatum's wife, Andrea Tatum, was found shot to death on March 20, 2014, in a Prince George's County, Maryland motel; Kahlil Tatum was found dead of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound on April 1, 2014, at Kenilworth Park and Aquatic Gardens in Northeast D.C.
The FBI and Metropolitan Police Department continue to offer a reward, now reported at up to $50,000, for information leading to Relisha's location or recovery.
D.C. police have stated the case remains open, with periodic public renewals of the search on anniversaries of her disappearance, including the case's 12th anniversary in March 2026.
unknown: Relisha's exact fate and the location of her remains, if she is in fact deceased as investigators believe, have never been established; no body has ever been found.

Why Relisha's prolonged absence from school went unreported by shelter staff and family for roughly 18 days has not been fully explained in any public accounting.
unanswered: What specifically happened to Relisha between the March 1, 2014 hotel sighting and Tatum's own death a month later?

name: Asha Degree
summary: Asha Degree, 9, disappeared from her family's home in Shelby, North Carolina in the early morning hours of February 14, 2000. Several motorists reported seeing her walking alone south along Highway 18 around 3:30–4:00 a.m. in heavy rain, carrying a backpack she had packed herself; when one driver slowed to approach her, she ran into the woods. Her parents discovered her missing later that morning. Eighteen months later, her backpack was found buried along the same highway, about 26 miles from her home. In 2024, investigators searched multiple properties belonging to a local family, seizing a vehicle matching a description linked to the night she disappeared, and increased the reward to $100,000; a person reportedly told police in 2024 that a member of that family had once said “I killed Asha Degree.” No arrest has ever been made, and Asha has never been found.
known: Asha's identity, age, and the February 14, 2000 disappearance, per the FBI's official case record and the Cleveland County Sheriff's Office.

Multiple motorists independently reported seeing a girl matching her description walking alone along Highway 18 in the predawn hours; one driver who slowed to approach her said she ran into a wooded area.
Asha's backpack, containing items including a children's book and a concert T-shirt, was found buried in a plastic bag along the same highway roughly 18 months later.

In September 2024 and again in 2026, investigators executed search warrants on properties belonging to the Dedmon family of Shelby, seizing a vehicle matching witness descriptions, VHS tapes, journals, and other items; the FBI and North Carolina SBI have named a member of that family as a person of interest.
The combined reward for information has grown to $100,000, and no arrest warrants have been issued as of the most recent public reporting.
unknown: Why Asha left her home in the middle of the night carrying a packed backpack has never been established.

The specific vehicle she may have entered, described as a dark green early-1970s Lincoln Mark IV or Ford Thunderbird, has not been conclusively confirmed as connected to a named suspect despite a similar vehicle being seized in the 2024 searches.
The full content of items seized in the 2024 and 2026 property searches, and what specifically they are alleged to show, has not been made public.
unanswered: Why did Asha leave her home on her own in the middle of the night, and where was she walking to?
What specifically has the seized vehicle and other evidence from the Dedmon family property searches shown investigators, and why has no arrest followed?
Is Asha still alive, as her family continues to hope, or was she killed shortly after her disappearance, as investigators have said they now believe?

name: Keeshae Jacobs
summary: Keeshae Jacobs, 21, disappeared in Richmond, Virginia after visiting a male friend's home on September 26, 2016. She texted her mother, Toni Jacobs, that she had arrived safely and would see her the next day; she was never heard from again. Richmond Police publicly stated in November 2017 that they believed foul play was involved, and in 2023 named a man, Otis Tucker, as a suspect in her disappearance; Tucker had given Jacobs's mother conflicting accounts of when he last saw her. In November 2022, Tucker was separately arrested and charged with second-degree murder and evidence tampering in the death of a different woman in Florida. He has never been charged in connection with Jacobs's disappearance. No arrest has been made and Keeshae has never been found.

name: Kierra Coles
summary: Kierra Coles, 26, a U.S. Postal Service letter carrier who was three months pregnant, disappeared from Chicago's Chatham neighborhood on October 2, 2018, after calling in sick to work. Surveillance footage that day showed her walking near her apartment in her postal uniform despite having called out; her car was later found parked on her block with her phone, purse, and lunch bag still inside. Chicago Police announced within two weeks that they suspected foul play. In 2022, police released additional surveillance video showing Coles withdrawing cash at a Walgreens ATM and driving off with a man identified as a person of interest shortly before her disappearance; that man was questioned but gave varying accounts and has never been arrested. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service raised its reward to $250,000 in 2026, the largest the agency offers. No arrest has ever been made and Coles has never been found.

name: Nakyla Williams
summary: Nakyla Williams, 24, a hairstylist who ran a salon out of her basement, disappeared in Indianapolis, Indiana on November 8, 2021, after a doorbell camera captured her getting into a loud, gray or white pickup truck outside her mother's home. She was later seen at a different residence that evening before leaving and never being heard from again. Her family identified a man named Bestin (or Destyn) Hoyle as the last person known to be with her; police sought him for questioning, though they have not classified him as a formal suspect. Her mother has said Hoyle left the state for Flint, Michigan shortly after Williams disappeared and deleted his social media interactions with her. Her family believes she may have been trafficked. No arrest has ever been made and Williams has never been found.

name: Jahi Turner
summary: Jahi Turner, 2, disappeared from a Golden Hill-area playground in San Diego on April 25, 2002, while in the care of his stepfather, Tieray Jones, whose 18-year-old Navy sailor wife was deployed at sea. Jones told police he left Jahi with a woman and other children at the park to buy a soda and returned to find them all gone; police found inconsistencies in his account but lacked evidence to charge him at the time. The case went cold for 14 years until new evidence, including a journal entry Jones wrote to his wife describing Jahi as unresponsive after a fall two days before he was reported missing, led to a murder charge in 2016. A 2018 jury deadlocked 10–2 in favor of acquittal on second-degree murder, and 10–2 in favor of conviction on the lesser charge of involuntary manslaughter; the judge declared a mistrial and later denied prosecutors' request for a second trial, finding it unlikely any future jury could reach a unanimous verdict given the missing body and 16-year delay. No one has ever been convicted, and Jahi has never been found.
known: Jahi's disappearance from a Golden Hill park on April 25, 2002, per San Diego police records and Jones's own account to investigators.
Police found inconsistencies in Jones's story in 2002 but lacked sufficient evidence to file charges at that time; the case remained open as a suspected homicide for over a decade.
Jones was arrested in North Carolina in 2016 after new evidence emerged, and charged with murder and felony child abuse causing death.
A journal entry Jones had written to his deployed wife, dated two days before he reported Jahi missing, described the toddler as unresponsive and not moving or talking after falling off a bed.
A 2018 jury deadlocked after deliberation, splitting 10–2 toward acquittal on second-degree murder and 10–2 toward conviction on involuntary manslaughter; the judge declared a mistrial.

Superior Court Judge Joan Weber denied the prosecution's request for a second trial in March 2018, stating the missing body and 16-year gap made it unlikely any future jury could reach a unanimous verdict, effectively ending the criminal case.
Jahi's body has never been found despite extensive searches, including of the Miramar landfill.
unknown: Whether Jahi died from an accidental injury that Jones then concealed, or was killed outright, has never been resolved — the judge herself said she could not rule out several different scenarios, including the possibility Jones's original story was true.

unanswered: What did the journal entry Jones wrote to his wife actually describe happening to Jahi, and why did it take 14 years to surface as evidence?

Is there any possibility of resolving the case through renewed forensic examination, given advances since the original 2002 investigation?

name: Anwar Green
summary: Anwar Green disappeared in Newark, New Jersey on January 19, 2001, after he and his friend Rahim Martin cashed a civil lawsuit settlement check for over $8,000 at a bank in downtown Newark. Surveillance footage showed Green appearing nervous and repeatedly glancing at the door inside the bank. The two men were last seen together at a nearby office building, where Martin briefly called his uncle from a lobby payphone without going up to see him. The day after the pair were reported missing, a man's burned and murdered body was found inside a deliberately set house fire in Newark; that body was identified as Martin in August 2010, nine years later, using DNA technology unavailable at the time of his death. No trace of Green has ever been found, and investigators believe both men were the victims of a robbery connected to the cash they were carrying.

name: Carolyn, Sheketah, Barry & Brandon Brown
summary: Carolyn Denise Brown, 27, and her three children — 10-year-old Sheketah, 6-year-old Barry, and 2-year-old Brandon — disappeared from their Port St. Lucie, Florida home in July 1985. Carolyn's mother alerted police in August after weeks without contact; officers found the home undisturbed at first glance, but Carolyn's purse held identification cut into pieces, an untouched meal sat on the dining table, and a freshly repainted wall concealed bloodstains beneath. Carolyn's husband and the children's father, James Michael Brown, later confessed in detail to killing all four, telling investigators where he said he disposed of each body — locations that were searched without any remains ever being recovered. Court-appointed psychiatrists diagnosed James as a paranoid schizophrenic experiencing hallucinations; a jury found him not guilty by reason of insanity in the deaths of Carolyn and Sheketah, and he was never separately charged for Barry and Brandon's deaths because their locations couldn't be confirmed. He was committed to a Florida mental health facility, later released to a halfway house, and was free by 1997. No family member has ever been found, and no one has ever been convicted of a crime in their deaths.

name: Tasha Shante Wright
summary: Tasha Shante Wright, 10, a gifted-and-talented fourth-grader, disappeared while walking a short distance within her own apartment complex in east Dallas, Texas on October 14, 1989. name: Barbara Jean Dreher
summary: Barbara Jean Dreher, 39, a mother of five who had worked as a Washington, D.C. public school secretary for fifteen years, disappeared on August 12, 1984 after dropping her two young sons off at her adult daughter's home, telling them she was going to pick up some money and would return shortly. Days later, her son spotted her burgundy Oldsmobile being driven by an unfamiliar man; he followed the car, called police, and identified the driver at the scene. Because the car had not been reported stolen, the man was released without arrest, though a ski mask, gloves, and rope were found inside the impounded vehicle. In 2018, D.C. police's cold case squad examined whether skeletal remains found in a Southeast D.C. apartment crawl space could be Dreher's, using DNA comparison; no match has been publicly confirmed. No one has ever been charged, and Barbara has never been found.

name: Dannette & Jeannette Millbrook
summary: Dannette and Jeannette Millbrook, 15-year-old fraternal twins, disappeared in Augusta, Georgia on March 18, 1990, after walking to a nearby gas station for snacks and telling their mother a man in a van had followed part of their route earlier that day. A gas station clerk was the last person to see them; nothing further is known about the man in the van. The Richmond County Sheriff's Office concluded the girls were runaways based on hearsay and closed the case in 1991, despite their mother's insistence they would not have left voluntarily. The case sat effectively unworked for over two decades until a newly elected sheriff reopened it in 2013; investigators have since interviewed witnesses, canvassed the area, and collected DNA samples from family members, but the case remains unsolved. Their case is believed to be one of the only unresolved disappearances of twins in American history.

name: Pshara Marie Jones
summary: Pshara Marie Jones, 20, a pharmacy employee, left her family's home in Claremore, Oklahoma on foot and without her phone on the evening of September 21, 2015, following an argument. Bank records show two transactions that same night, including one at a convenience store, but no account activity since. She never returned for medication she took for a mental health condition and never showed up for her next shift at the pharmacy where she worked. Her mother did not report her missing for roughly two weeks, initially expecting her to return or call as she reportedly had after past arguments. The Claremore Police Department's chief investigator has stated publicly that investigators strongly believe foul play was involved. No arrest has ever been made and Pshara has never been found.
known: Pshara's identity, age, and the September 21, 2015 disappearance following an argument at her family's home, per the Claremore Police Department and NamUs case record.

name: The Clinton Avenue Five
summary: Melvin Pittman, 17, Ernest Taylor, 17, Alvin Turner, 16, Randy Johnson, 16, and Michael McDowell, 16 — five teenagers known as the Clinton Avenue Five — vanished together in Newark, New Jersey on August 20, 1978, after playing basketball and getting into a pickup truck driven by Lee Anthony Evans, a local handyman who paid them in odd jobs. The case went cold as a missing-persons file for three decades until 2008, when Evans's cousin Philander Hampton, in police custody on an unrelated charge, confessed after a 13-hour interrogation that Evans had lured the boys to a vacant house, locked them in a closet at gunpoint over a stolen-marijuana dispute, and set the building on fire, killing all five. Hampton pleaded guilty and received a 10-year sentence plus $15,000 in relocation money in exchange for testifying against Evans. At Evans's 2011 trial, where he represented himself, a jury acquitted him of all ten murder-related charges, finding the prosecution's case — built almost entirely on Hampton's confession, with no bodies or physical evidence ever recovered — insufficient. No one has ever been convicted of killing the five boys, whose remains have never been found.
known: The five teenagers' identities, ages, and the August 20, 1978 disappearance after boarding Evans's pickup truck, per Wikipedia's sourced case history and contemporaneous reporting.

In November 2008, Philander Hampton confessed after a 13-hour police interrogation that he and his cousin, Lee Anthony Evans, lured the boys to a vacant house at 256 Camden Street, locked them in a third-floor closet at gunpoint, and burned the building down with them inside.
Sonar searches of the fire site, conducted after Hampton's confession, found no human remains.
Evans and Hampton were arrested and charged with felony murder and arson in March 2010.
Hampton pleaded guilty and received a 10-year prison sentence and $15,000 in relocation money in exchange for testifying against Evans.
A jury acquitted Evans, who represented himself at trial, of all ten murder-related charges in November 2011, finding the prosecution had not proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt.

Evans later filed a federal civil suit against the Essex County prosecutor's office and Newark police alleging his confession-based prosecution relied on coerced testimony and fabricated evidence; a federal appeals panel ruled in 2025 that the detectives involved were not entitled to qualified immunity from that suit.

name: Anthony Lamar Smith
summary: Anthony Lamar Smith, 24, was shot and killed by St. Louis Police Officer Jason Stockley on December 20, 2011, after a high-speed chase that began when Stockley believed he witnessed a drug transaction outside a Church's Chicken. Dashcam audio captured Stockley telling his partner “we're killing this [expletive], don't you know it” less than a minute before shooting Smith five times. Prosecutors alleged Stockley then planted a revolver in Smith's car — only Stockley's DNA was found on the gun, not Smith's. Stockley was charged with first-degree murder in 2016 and chose to have his case decided by a judge rather than a jury; in September 2017, Circuit Judge Timothy Wilson acquitted him, writing the state had not proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt and remarking that “an urban heroin dealer not in possession of a firearm would be an anomaly.” No one has ever been convicted in Smith's death.
known: The chase, the shooting, and Smith's death, per dashcam footage and evidence presented at Stockley's 2017 bench trial.
Dashcam audio captured Stockley saying “we're killing this [expletive], don't you know it” approximately one minute before he shot Smith five times.

In-car camera footage showed Stockley returning to his SUV and searching through a duffel bag immediately after the shooting; prosecutors alleged he retrieved a revolver from that bag to plant in Smith's car.
DNA testing found Stockley's DNA on the gun recovered from Smith's car, and did not find Smith's.

Stockley requested a bench trial rather than a jury trial, over prosecutors' objection; Circuit Judge Timothy Wilson acquitted him of first-degree murder and armed criminal action in September 2017, ruling the state had not disproven self-defense beyond a reasonable doubt.
The acquittal prompted sustained protests in downtown St. Louis, including dozens of arrests.
unknown: Whether Stockley in fact planted the gun in Smith's car, as prosecutors alleged based on the DNA evidence and his return to the duffel bag, was never resolved by any conviction — the judge found the evidence insufficient to disprove self-defense regardless.

unanswered: Why did DNA testing find only Stockley's DNA, not Smith's, on the gun recovered from Smith's car?

Why did Judge Wilson choose to credit an inference about drug dealers generally, rather than evidence specific to this case, in his written ruling?

name: Christian Taylor
summary: Christian Taylor, 19, an Angelo State University football player, was shot and killed by rookie Arlington, Texas Police Officer Brad Miller on August 7, 2015, inside a car dealership showroom he had broken into and was vandalizing while, an autopsy later showed, under the influence of a hallucinogen. Miller broke from his training officer and entered the showroom alone without informing his supervisor, then shot Taylor, who was unarmed, four times as Taylor advanced toward him after refusing to get on the ground. Miller was fired days later for what the police chief called a “catastrophic” tactical decision to confront Taylor alone. A Tarrant County grand jury declined to indict Miller in June 2016. No one has ever been charged in Taylor's death.
known: The break-in, the confrontation, and the shooting, per Arlington Police Chief Will Johnson's public statements and dealership surveillance video of Taylor's behavior beforehand.
Miller entered the showroom alone, without informing his supervising officer, rather than helping establish a perimeter as instructed.

Miller's training officer, who followed him into the showroom, deployed a Taser that failed to stop Taylor before Miller fired his service weapon four times.
Miller was fired four days after the shooting; Chief Johnson said Miller's tactical decisions led to “cascading consequences” resulting in the shooting.
A Tarrant County grand jury declined to indict Miller on any charge on June 8, 2016.
The City of Arlington approved an $850,000 settlement with Taylor's family in May 2017.
unknown: The precise sequence of Taylor's advance toward Miller, and whether verbal commands were given the opportunity to work before Miller fired, was described only through police and Miller's own account, since no video exists of the shooting itself.
Why Miller chose to enter alone rather than wait for backup, given ten other officers were reportedly in the vicinity, has not been fully explained beyond the department's internal review.

name: Kajieme Powell
summary: Kajieme Powell, 25, was shot and killed by St. Louis Police Officers Nicholas Shelton and Ellis Brown outside a convenience store on August 19, 2014 — ten days after the shooting of Michael Brown in nearby Ferguson. Officers responding to a report of shoplifting and a man carrying a knife found Powell, who witnesses said was in mental distress; a bystander's cellphone video showed police firing 12 shots roughly 23 seconds after arriving on scene, as Powell advanced holding what a later analysis confirmed was a knife. St. Louis Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce reviewed forensic evidence, witness accounts, and a 3-D spatial reconstruction before announcing in November 2015 that no charges would be filed, concluding a criminal violation could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. A use-of-force expert later hired by Powell's family disputed the analysis Joyce's office relied on. No one has ever been charged in Powell's death.
known: The shooting, the roughly 23-second timeframe from officers' arrival to gunfire, and Powell's death, per bystander cellphone video and the St. Louis Circuit Attorney's 40-page public report.
911 callers reported Powell had stolen items from the store and was carrying a knife, though no caller reported he appeared to be experiencing a mental health crisis.

Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce's office reviewed forensic, video, 911, dispatch, and witness evidence along with a third-party 3-D spatial analysis before concluding in November 2015 that a criminal violation against either officer could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

A separate force analysis commissioned in 2015 by a Washington University professor and shared with both prosecutors and the family's attorney disputed the circuit attorney's application of standard use-of-force distance calculations, arguing officers who already had weapons drawn needed less reaction time than the analysis assumed.
Powell's mother filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the city and the two named officers in federal court.
unknown: Whether Powell was experiencing a mental health crisis that officers could have de-escalated differently, as his family's attorney has argued, was not resolved by the circuit attorney's charging decision.

The specific weight given to the disputed 3-D spatial and use-of-force analyses in the circuit attorney's final conclusion has been challenged by outside experts but not independently re-examined by any court.
What internal disciplinary review, if any, the two officers faced separate from the criminal charging decision has not been made comprehensively public.

What became of Karen Powell's federal wrongful death lawsuit against the city and the officers?
What crisis-intervention training, if any, did the responding officers have, given witness accounts describing Powell as in mental distress?

name: VonDerrit Myers Jr.
summary: VonDerrit Myers Jr., 18, was shot and killed by an off-duty St. Louis police officer, Jason Flanery, working a private security patrol job on October 8, 2014, in the city's Shaw neighborhood — exactly two months after Michael Brown's death in nearby Ferguson. Police said Myers ran from the officer, then turned and fired three shots at him during a foot chase before Flanery returned fire, striking Myers multiple times; a stolen 9mm handgun was recovered at the scene. Myers's family disputed that he was armed at the moment he was shot and said the investigation contained inconsistencies. St. Louis Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce reviewed the case independently of a grand jury and announced in May 2015 that criminal charges could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. No one has ever been charged in Myers's death.

name: Quintonio LeGrier & Bettie Jones
summary: Quintonio LeGrier, 19, a Northern Illinois University student experiencing a mental health crisis, and Bettie Jones, 55, his family's downstairs neighbor, were both shot and killed by Chicago Police Officer Robert Rialmo on December 26, 2015, while responding to a domestic disturbance call. Jones opened her door to direct officers upstairs; LeGrier came down the stairs swinging an aluminum bat, and Rialmo fired eight shots, six striking LeGrier and one accidentally striking Jones, whom police immediately acknowledged was an innocent bystander. The Cook County State's Attorney's Office declined to bring criminal charges in 2017, finding insufficient evidence to disprove self-defense. The city's own police oversight agency later found Rialmo's account “inconsistent and ultimately unreliable” and recommended his firing; the Chicago Police Board unanimously fired him in 2019, though only over the Jones shooting — a separate civil jury found the LeGrier shooting itself justified. No one has ever been criminally charged in either death.

Rialmo fired eight shots, striking LeGrier six times and Jones once; the department acknowledged Jones was shot by mistake.

name: Willie McCoy
summary: Willie McCoy, 20, a local rapper, was shot and killed by six Vallejo, California police officers who fired 55 rounds at him in 3.5 seconds on February 9, 2019, after he was found asleep behind the wheel of his car in a Taco Bell drive-thru with a handgun in his lap. Officers surrounded the vehicle; when McCoy stirred awake, they said he reached for the gun, and all six opened fire, striking him roughly 25 times. The Solano County District Attorney recused her office, and a special prosecutor concluded in January 2021 that all six officers acted in lawful self-defense. An independent use-of-force report commissioned by the city separately found the shooting “reasonable and necessary,” though the police chief internally recommended firing one of the six officers for unsafe firearm handling that endangered his colleagues — the only consequence any officer faced. No one has ever been criminally charged in McCoy's death.
known: The welfare-check call, the 55 shots fired in 3.5 seconds, and McCoy's death, per an independent use-of-force report commissioned by the City of Vallejo and body camera footage released by police.
McCoy had a stolen handgun in his lap when officers arrived; police said he reached for it when he woke up, prompting the six officers to open fire.

Solano County District Attorney Krishna Abrams recused her office from the case; special prosecutor Michael Ramos, a former San Bernardino County district attorney, concluded in January 2021 that all six officers were legally justified.
An independent use-of-force report, prepared by a consultant retained by the city, found the officers' actions “objectively reasonable and necessary.”

Vallejo Police Chief Shawny Williams internally recommended firing Officer Ryan McMahon in March 2020, finding his firearm handling during the shooting endangered other officers on scene and violated department policy; McMahon had also fatally shot another man, Ronell Foster, in 2018 without facing discipline.
McMahon was formally fired in 2020 — the only disciplinary consequence any of the six officers faced, and unconnected to any criminal charge.
unknown: Whether McCoy was in fact reaching for the gun, versus simply waking up disoriented, was disputed by the family's attorney, who called the response “overkill” and “unnecessary,” and has never been resolved by any criminal proceeding.

Why six officers firing 55 rounds at a man seated in a parked car was found reasonable by both the special prosecutor and the city's own hired use-of-force expert, when McCoy's family disputed that characterization, has not been reconciled.
The same use-of-force expert who reviewed this shooting had also found the officers justified in the unrelated fatal shooting of Stephon Clark, a pattern the family's attorney publicly questioned.
unanswered: Why did it take nearly two years for a charging decision to be reached after the district attorney's recusal?
Why was Officer McMahon kept on the force after his 2018 shooting of Ronell Foster, only to be involved in a second fatal shooting the following year?
What specific department-wide changes, if any, did Vallejo implement given its documented status as one of the region's highest per-capita rates of police shootings?

name: Marcus-David Peters
summary: Marcus-David Peters, 24, a high school biology teacher, was shot and killed by Richmond, Virginia Police Officer Michael Nyantakyi on May 14, 2018, during a mental health crisis. Peters struck several vehicles with his car, crashed near an Interstate 95 ramp, then emerged naked and unarmed and ran into rush-hour highway traffic, where he was struck by a passing car. Body camera video showed him lying in the road, rolling and moving his limbs, before getting up and running toward Nyantakyi shouting threats; the officer deployed a Taser without effect, then fired his service weapon. Richmond's Commonwealth's Attorney found the shooting a “justifiable homicide” months later in 2018, and a successor prosecutor who reopened the case at the family's request reached the identical conclusion in 2020. No one has ever been charged in Peters's death, and his name has become a lasting symbol of Richmond's police reform movement.
known: The car crash, Peters's naked and unarmed state, and the shooting on the I-95/64 ramp, per Richmond Police body camera footage and the Commonwealth's Attorney's public reports.
Nyantakyi, who is also Black, first deployed a Taser, which appeared to have no effect, before firing his service weapon as Peters ran toward him shouting threats.
Commonwealth's Attorney Michael Herring released a 15-page report in August 2018 concluding the shooting was reasonable and necessary and declining to charge Nyantakyi.

A relative of Peters admitted to removing and disposing of a Ritalin prescription bottle from his apartment after his death, according to Herring's report; toxicology found THC and Ritalin in Peters's system.

In 2020, successor Commonwealth's Attorney Colette McEachin agreed to review the case again at the urging of Peters's family and reform advocates, and reached the same conclusion in a 10-page report: the shooting was a reasonable response to the danger Peters posed.
Peters's sister, Princess Blanding, became a prominent police-reform advocate following his death and later ran for governor of Virginia.

What specific de-escalation options, if any, existed between the Taser's ineffectiveness and the use of a firearm has been debated by outside police-practice observers but not resolved by either prosecutorial review.

What specifically led a family member to remove and dispose of medication from Peters's apartment after his death, and how did that affect the investigation's toxicology findings?
What crisis-intervention training did Nyantakyi have prior to the encounter, and did Richmond's police department change that training as a result of this case?

name: Ronell Foster
summary: Ronell Foster, 33, a father of two, was shot and killed by Vallejo, California Police Officer Ryan McMahon on February 13, 2018, after McMahon tried to stop him for riding his bicycle without a headlight. Foster fled on foot after a chase; McMahon Tased him twice without effect, struck him repeatedly with a metal flashlight — including at least one blow to the head, which McMahon later admitted was a use of deadly force — and, after Foster grabbed the flashlight, shot him seven times, including once in the head and four times in the back. The Solano County District Attorney's Office cleared McMahon of criminal charges in January 2020, nearly two years later, finding the shooting justified. McMahon was the same officer who, thirteen months after killing Foster, was one of six Vallejo officers who fired 55 rounds at Willie McCoy in a Taco Bell drive-thru. No one has ever been charged in Foster's death.

The Solano County District Attorney's Office announced in January 2020 that it could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that McMahon's use of force was not justified, citing his account that Foster grabbed the flashlight and presented it in a threatening manner; body camera footage did not clearly show that alleged threat, per contemporaneous reporting.

Internal Vallejo Police Department reviews reached conflicting conclusions: the internal affairs sergeant who investigated initially cleared McMahon of policy violations, while both the department's deputy chief and interim chief who ordered a later review disagreed.

The City of Vallejo settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Foster's family for $5.7 million, reported as the largest settlement in the city's history at the time.

Why the same officer was permitted to remain on active duty after this shooting, going on to participate in the fatal shooting of Willie McCoy thirteen months later, has not been addressed in any official public accounting beyond his eventual firing over the McCoy incident specifically.
unanswered: Why did prosecutors and internal investigators reach different conclusions about whether McMahon's conduct was within policy, and why was the more critical internal assessment not acted on sooner?
What specifically changed between McMahon's clearance in this case and his firing over the McCoy shooting a year later, given both involved similar allegations of unsafe conduct?

name: Mansur Ball-Bey
summary: Mansur Ball-Bey, 18, was shot and killed by St. Louis Police Officers Kyle Chandler and Ronald Vaughan while they were serving a search warrant in the Fountain Park neighborhood on August 19, 2015. Police said Ball-Bey pointed a gun at officers as he ran out the back door of the home being searched; his family disputed he was armed at all. St. Louis Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce declined to charge either officer in June 2016, citing insufficient evidence to disprove self-defense. In February 2025, nearly a decade later, a federal jury in a wrongful death lawsuit rejected the officers' account, awarding Ball-Bey's family $18.75 million after deliberating for just 90 minutes. As of August 2025, the city still had not paid the judgment. No one has ever been criminally charged in Ball-Bey's death.
known: The search warrant, the shooting, and Ball-Bey's death, per the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department's Force Investigative Unit and the Circuit Attorney's public report.
Officer Kyle Chandler fired the fatal shot; Officer Ronald Vaughan also fired but did not strike Ball-Bey.

Circuit Attorney Jennifer Joyce announced in June 2016 that a criminal violation against either officer could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt, citing a lack of an independent witness who contradicted the officers' account.
A pistol was recovered in the backyard near a dumpster; an off-duty officer who witnessed the chase testified Ball-Bey tossed the weapon there, and police said his fingerprints were found on it.
Ball-Bey's father filed a federal wrongful death lawsuit in 2020 against the officers, the former police chief, and the city.

A federal jury deliberated for approximately 90 minutes in February 2025 before awarding Ball-Bey's family $6.25 million in compensatory damages and $12.5 million in punitive damages, totaling $18.75 million; as of the case's tenth anniversary in August 2025, the city had not yet paid the judgment.
unknown: Whether Ball-Bey pointed a weapon at officers before he was shot, as police maintained, or was unarmed at that moment, as his family long argued, was never resolved by any criminal proceeding; the swift, decisive federal civil verdict against the officers a decade later suggests a jury did not find the police account credible, though that verdict addressed civil liability, not criminal guilt.

Whether the recovered pistol was in fact Ball-Bey's or was, as some attorneys and community members alleged based on the officers' prior history, planted evidence has never been independently established.
Why federal records showed Ball-Bey had not been to his job in at least 24 hours before the shooting, contradicting an early account that he had just come from work, has not been explained.
unanswered: Why did it take a federal civil jury just 90 minutes to reject the officers' account, when the criminal charging decision nearly a decade earlier concluded the same account could not be disproven beyond a reasonable doubt?
Has the city of St. Louis paid the $18.75 million judgment, and if not, why not, as of the case's tenth anniversary?
What became of a since-revealed city audit reportedly showing multiple errors across dozens of St. Louis police shooting investigations, and did Ball-Bey's case factor into that finding?

name: Stephon Watts
summary: Stephon Watts, 15, who was diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome and ADHD, was shot and killed in his own basement by Calumet City, Illinois police officers on February 1, 2012, after his father called the department's non-emergency line for help during an argument over school — following prior advice from social workers to call police when Stephon became agitated. Police had responded to the home at least ten times over the previous two years, and the address was flagged as belonging to a person with a disability. Officers said Stephon lunged at them with a steak knife; his father maintained it was only a butter knife. Two officers fired, killing him within roughly two minutes of entering the home. Cook County's State's Attorney cleared both officers of any misconduct that April, and a decade-long civil suit ended in 2022 when an Illinois appellate court ruled the officers were legally immune from liability. No officer was ever criminally charged, disciplined, or fired.
known: The non-emergency call, the responding officers' prior familiarity with Stephon's autism diagnosis, and the shooting roughly two minutes after officers entered the home, per Cook County State's Attorney's Office records and the family's civil suit filings.
Police had responded to the Watts home at least ten times in the two years before the shooting, and the address carried a code indicating a resident with a disability lived there.

Officers said Stephon lunged at them twice with a knife, cutting one officer's forearm before a second officer fired; anonymous police sources described the weapon as a nine-inch steak knife, while Stephon's father maintained throughout that it was only a butter knife.
The Cook County State's Attorney's Office cleared both officers of any criminal conduct in April 2012.

Stephon's mother, Danelene Powell-Watts, filed a civil negligence suit against the city and the two officers; in 2022, the Illinois Court of Appeals affirmed a lower court ruling that the officers were statutorily immune from liability, finding their conduct did not rise to “willful and wanton” behavior.
No officer involved was ever criminally charged, internally disciplined, or fired as a result of the shooting.
unknown: Whether the knife Stephon held was in fact the nine-inch steak knife anonymous police sources described or the butter knife his father maintained was the only weapon in the house has never been independently and publicly resolved.

Given ten prior police contacts at the home, including at least one where officers used a Taser to de-escalate without lethal force, why officers escalated to gunfire within roughly two minutes on this occasion has not been fully explained.
What specific crisis-intervention or disability-awareness training, if any, the responding officers had received prior to this documented, coded address has not been made public.
unanswered: Why did officers who had responded to this specific, flagged address at least ten times before — and had used a Taser to de-escalate on a prior occasion — resort to lethal force within roughly two minutes on this call?

What specifically justified the appellate court's finding that the officers' conduct did not rise to “willful and wanton” behavior, given the family called specifically for help rather than enforcement?
What changes, if any, has Calumet City made to how it dispatches officers to addresses flagged for a resident's disability since this case?

name: Dontre Hamilton
summary: Dontre Hamilton, 31, who had schizophrenia, was shot 13 or 14 times and killed by Milwaukee Police Officer Christopher Manney at Red Arrow Park on April 30, 2014, after Manney conducted a pat-down search while responding to a call about a man sleeping in the park. Manney said Hamilton grabbed his baton and attacked him, prompting him to open fire. Milwaukee County District Attorney John Chisholm declined to charge Manney in December 2014, finding the shooting was self-defense. The U.S. Department of Justice separately reviewed the case and declined federal charges in November 2015. Police Chief Edward Flynn fired Manney months before either declination — not for the shooting itself, but for conducting a pat-down that violated department policy and escalated the encounter; that firing was later upheld through two rounds of appeal. No one has ever been criminally charged in Hamilton's death.
known: The pat-down, the struggle over Manney's baton, and the shooting, per Milwaukee County District Attorney John Chisholm's public report and an independent state investigation.
Witnesses said Hamilton held the baton in an “aggressive posture” before Manney fired; Chisholm's report noted witnesses said Manney stopped firing once Hamilton fell.
District Attorney Chisholm announced in December 2014 that Manney was justified in using deadly force in self-defense, declining to bring charges.

The U.S. Department of Justice, after conducting its own investigation with the FBI, announced in November 2015 that there was insufficient evidence to charge Manney with a federal civil rights violation.

Police Chief Edward Flynn fired Manney in October 2014, before either charging decision, explicitly for violating department pat-down policy in a way that escalated what should have been a routine welfare check — not for the shooting itself.
Manney's firing was upheld by Milwaukee's Fire and Police Commission, a circuit court judge, and the Wisconsin Court of Appeals across successive appeals.
The shooting prompted the Milwaukee Police Department to equip officers with body cameras.
unknown: Whether Hamilton's actions with the baton constituted the kind of “deadly attack” Chisholm's report described, versus a reflexive reaction to an unnecessary pat-down while sleeping, was disputed by the family and has never been tested at any criminal trial.
The specific number of shots fired — reported as either 13 or 14 depending on the source — reflects a minor but persistent discrepancy across official accounts.

Why Hamilton, whom his family said was not violent and was experiencing a mental health episode, was patted down at all during what began as a welfare check has been disputed by the family even though the department itself found the pat-down improper.
unanswered: If the department's own chief found the initial pat-down violated policy and directly caused the escalation that led to the shooting, why did both the county and federal reviews still conclude the shooting itself was legally justified self-defense?
What specific de-escalation or mental-health-crisis training changes did the Milwaukee Police Department implement as a direct result of this case, beyond body cameras?
What became of Manney professionally after his firing was fully upheld through the appeals process?

name: Jerame Reid
summary: Jerame Reid, 36, was shot and killed by Bridgeton, New Jersey Police Officer Braheme Days on December 30, 2014, moments after Reid stepped out of a car with his hands raised during a traffic stop for running a stop sign. Dashcam video, released publicly in January 2015, showed Days and his partner Roger Worley ordering Reid to stay in the vehicle and not move; Reid exited anyway with his hands up, and Days opened fire, striking him fatally as Worley also fired but missed. A Cumberland County grand jury declined to indict either officer in May 2015. Federal prosecutors separately reviewed the case and announced in August 2016 that the evidence was insufficient to bring civil rights charges. No one has ever been charged in Reid's death.
known: The traffic stop, Reid exiting the vehicle with his hands raised, and the shooting, captured in full on the patrol car's dashcam and released publicly in January 2015.
Officer Braheme Days fired the fatal shot; Officer Roger Worley also fired but did not strike Reid.
Days had arrested Reid months earlier, in August 2014, and recognized him during the stop; Reid had served roughly 13 years in prison as a teenager for shooting at state troopers.

Nine prior municipal court complaints had been filed against Days between 2012 and the shooting alleging he stopped, searched, or charged people without cause; all were dismissed for lack of probable cause.

A Cumberland County grand jury declined to indict either officer on May 1, 2015; the family's attorney publicly stated the prosecutor's press release on the decision omitted the officers' own statements, autopsy results, and their prior use-of-force complaint history.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey announced on August 22, 2016 that federal civil rights charges were not warranted, finding insufficient evidence that Days acted with willful criminal intent.
Cumberland County settled a federal wrongful death lawsuit with Reid's widow for $340,000.
unknown: Why Days opened fire on Reid, who was visibly complying by raising his hands as he exited the vehicle — as opposed to the driver, who exited the same way without incident — has never been resolved beyond Days's own account that he feared for his life.

The full autopsy results and officer statements that the family's attorney said were omitted from the prosecutor's public announcement of the grand jury's decision have not been comprehensively made public in the years since.
Whether Days's prior use-of-force complaint history factored into either the grand jury's or federal prosecutors' review has not been detailed publicly.
unanswered: Why was Reid shot for exiting the vehicle with his hands raised when the driver, doing the same thing, was taken into custody without incident?

Why did the Cumberland County prosecutor's public release on the grand jury's decision omit the officers' statements, autopsy results, and Days's prior complaint history, as the family's attorney alleged?
What became of the nine prior municipal complaints against Officer Days, and did any internal review connect that pattern to this shooting?

name: Jamar Clark
summary: Jamar Clark, 24, was shot in the head by Minneapolis Police Officer Dustin Schwarze on November 15, 2015, during a struggle after officers responded to a report that Clark had assaulted his girlfriend and interfered with paramedics. Witnesses at the scene told police and reporters Clark was handcuffed when he was shot; the shooting sparked an 18-day protest encampment outside the police department's Fourth Precinct. Hennepin County Attorney Mike Freeman, bypassing the customary use of a grand jury, announced in March 2016 that DNA evidence and the absence of bruising on Clark's wrists showed he was not handcuffed and had grabbed at an officer's gun, and declined to bring charges. The U.S. Attorney's Office separately declined federal civil rights charges months later, and the police department cleared both officers of any policy violation. No one has ever been charged in Clark's death.
known: The struggle and the shooting, per the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension's investigation and Hennepin County Attorney Mike Freeman's detailed public presentation of the evidence.
Multiple eyewitnesses at the scene told police and media that Clark was handcuffed when he was shot; other witnesses gave conflicting accounts, some saying his hands were up or he was lying still.

Freeman announced in March 2016 that DNA testing found no trace of Clark's DNA on the handcuffs and no bruising consistent with cuffing on his wrists, and that officer Ringgenberg reported feeling Clark's hand move his holstered gun during the struggle.

Freeman broke from the county's prior practice of using a secret grand jury for police-shooting decisions, instead announcing the charging decision himself after a lengthy public presentation of evidence.
The U.S. Attorney's Office for Minnesota announced in June 2016 that there was insufficient evidence to bring federal civil rights charges against officers Ringgenberg and Schwarze.
Minneapolis Police Chief Janee Harteau publicly stated she supported the officers' actions after an internal review found no policy violation, meaning neither officer faced any discipline.
unknown: Why so many witnesses at the scene independently reported seeing Clark handcuffed, directly contradicting the forensic conclusions Freeman's office relied on, has never been reconciled.

Whether Clark in fact reached for the officer's gun, as Ringgenberg reported feeling during the struggle, or whether the physical evidence supporting that account could be explained another way, was disputed by community members who reviewed the same presentation.
No video captured the shooting itself with sufficient clarity to independently resolve either account, despite some cellphone footage of the aftermath.
unanswered: Why did so many bystander witness accounts describing Clark as handcuffed conflict so starkly with the forensic evidence the county attorney's office presented?
Why did the police department's own internal review clear both officers of any policy violation without any independent public accounting of its methodology?
What specific reforms, if any, did Minneapolis implement regarding grand jury practices for police shootings following Freeman's decision to handle this case differently?

name: Jason Harrison
summary: Jason Harrison, 38, who had bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, was shot five times and killed by Dallas Police Officers John Rogers and Andrew Hutchins on June 14, 2014, within seconds of appearing in his own doorway holding a screwdriver. His mother, Shirley Harrison, had called 911 asking for trained officers to help take her son — off his medication and in crisis — to a hospital, and told the dispatcher he was bipolar and schizophrenic. Body camera footage, the first in Dallas to capture a fatal police shooting, showed officers ordering Harrison to drop the screwdriver before shooting him five times, twice in the back, as his mother screamed for them to stop. A Dallas County grand jury declined to indict either officer in April 2015, and a federal judge dismissed the family's civil rights lawsuit in 2016, ruling the shooting did not violate Harrison's constitutional rights. No one has ever been charged in Harrison's death.
known: The 911 call, Harrison's mental health history, and the shooting, per body camera footage released by the Dallas Police Department and the family's federal lawsuit.
Harrison's mother told the 911 dispatcher he was bipolar and schizophrenic, off his medication, and asked specifically for trained officers to help take him to a hospital.
Officers shot Harrison five times, including twice in the back, within roughly five to eight seconds of his appearance in the doorway holding a screwdriver.
A Dallas County grand jury declined to indict Officers John Rogers and Andrew Hutchins on any charge in April 2015.
Neither officer attempted to use a Taser or other non-lethal option before resorting to gunfire, per the family's lawsuit and body camera footage.

U.S. District Judge David Godbey dismissed the family's federal civil rights lawsuit in March 2016, ruling the body camera video showed Harrison lunged at the officers and that the shooting did not violate his constitutional rights.
unknown: Whether Harrison in fact lunged at officers in a threatening manner, as the officers' attorney maintained and the federal judge found supported by the video, or whether he was attempting to comply and simply startled, as the family's attorney argued watching the same footage, remains disputed — the case never reached a jury.

Why officers did not attempt a Taser or other non-lethal method, despite dispatchers having relayed Harrison's specific mental health diagnoses in advance, has not been fully explained by the department.

Whether Dallas Police Department crisis-intervention training in effect at the time addressed encounters with someone already known to be in a documented mental health crisis has not been comprehensively detailed publicly.
unanswered: Why did officers who were told in advance that Harrison was bipolar and schizophrenic not attempt any non-lethal option before firing within seconds of his appearance?
Why did being shot twice in the back factor into neither the grand jury's decision nor the federal judge's dismissal of the civil case?
What specific changes to Dallas Police Department's mental-health-crisis response training, if any, followed this case, given the family's stated goal of reform?

name: Alfred Olango
summary: Alfred Olango, 38, a Ugandan refugee who had lived in the U.S. since childhood, was shot and killed by El Cajon, California Police Officer Richard Gonsalves on September 27, 2016, within about two minutes of officers arriving in response to his sister's 911 call reporting he was mentally ill, unarmed, and having an emotional breakdown after a close friend's death. Officers said Olango pulled an object from his pocket, assumed “what appeared to be a shooting stance,” and pointed it at Gonsalves, who fired four times as a second officer simultaneously deployed a Taser; the object turned out to be a vape pen. San Diego County District Attorney Bonnie Dumanis declined to charge Gonsalves in January 2017, finding the shooting legally justified. A 2019 civil jury also cleared Gonsalves of negligence. No one has ever been criminally charged in Olango's death.
known: The 911 call from Olango's sister, describing him as mentally ill and unarmed, and the shooting roughly two minutes after officers arrived, per the El Cajon Police Department and San Diego County District Attorney's public findings.
The object Olango drew from his pocket was a vape smoking device (a Pioneer for You Vape), not a weapon, per the El Cajon Police Department's own evidence release.

District Attorney Bonnie Dumanis announced in January 2017 that Gonsalves acted lawfully, concluding Olango's motion with the vape pen was a purposeful act intended to make the officer fear he was about to be shot.
Officer Gonsalves had been demoted the year before the shooting following an unrelated sexual harassment lawsuit, and was never relieved of duty following Olango's death.
A 2019 civil jury deliberated approximately one hour before unanimously finding Gonsalves not negligent in a wrongful death suit brought by Olango's sister, who witnessed the shooting.
U.S. immigration authorities had twice attempted to deport Olango in the years before his death but were unable to, since Uganda would not accept him back.
unknown: Whether Olango's exact hand movement with the vape pen was, as the district attorney concluded, a deliberate act meant to provoke fear of being shot, or an ambiguous gesture by a man in visible mental distress, was disputed by the family's attorney and never tested at a criminal trial.
Full, unedited bystander video of the incident, which police said corroborated their account, was not made public in its entirety, per contemporaneous reporting.

Whether officers' roughly hour-long response time to the initial 911 call, during which Olango continued walking in traffic and behaving erratically, affected the outcome once they finally arrived has not been directly addressed in any official finding.
unanswered: Why did officers, informed in advance that Olango was mentally ill and unarmed, escalate to lethal force within two minutes of arriving rather than attempting sustained de-escalation?
Why was Officer Gonsalves never relieved of duty following the shooting, despite a recent unrelated demotion for misconduct?
What specific crisis-intervention training changes, if any, did the El Cajon Police Department implement as a result of this case?

name: India Kager
summary: India Kager, 27, a Navy veteran, mother, and U.S. Postal Service worker, was shot and killed by Virginia Beach SWAT officers on September 5, 2015, when they opened fire on her car in a 7-Eleven parking lot after her passenger, Angelo Perry — the father of her four-month-old son, who was in the backseat — fired at approaching officers. Police, who had been surveilling Perry as a homicide suspect, fired approximately 30 rounds into the vehicle within about nine seconds; Kager had no criminal history and no known involvement in Perry's activities. Her infant son survived uninjured. Virginia Beach's Commonwealth's Attorney declined to charge any of the four officers in March 2016, calling the shooting justified and confirming Kager herself was not engaged in any illegal activity. In 2018, a civil jury found two of the four officers liable for gross negligence, awarding her family $800,000. No one has ever been criminally charged in Kager's death.
known: The surveillance of Perry, the confrontation in the 7-Eleven parking lot, and the approximately 30 rounds fired into the vehicle, per Virginia Beach Commonwealth's Attorney Colin Stolle's public findings and subsequent civil trial testimony.

Perry fired first at officers; four SWAT officers returned fire, and Kager was struck by an estimated seven or eight bullets, some of which may have passed through Perry's body first, per autopsy findings.

Commonwealth's Attorney Stolle announced in March 2016 that no charges would be filed against any of the four officers, while separately confirming there was no information that Kager herself was involved in any illegal activity.
Kager and Perry's four-month-old son, in the backseat throughout the shooting, was unharmed and briefly placed in the care of Child Protective Services.

Kager's parents filed a $15 million wrongful death lawsuit against the officers in 2017; in August 2018 a civil jury found two of the four officers grossly negligent and awarded the family $800,000, while clearing the other two officers.
Kager's case became part of the African American Policy Forum's #SayHerName campaign, which highlights Black women killed by police whose cases receive comparatively less public attention.
unknown: Whether officers took adequate account of Kager's presence and her infant son's presence in the vehicle before opening fire with roughly 30 rounds has never been resolved beyond the split civil verdict finding two of four officers grossly negligent.
The precise number of the 30 rounds fired that struck Kager directly, versus those that passed through Perry first, was estimated from autopsy evidence but not established with certainty.

Why the criminal review concluded the shooting was fully justified while a later civil jury found half the officers involved grossly negligent over the same underlying conduct has not been reconciled in any single public accounting.
unanswered: Why did prosecutors conclude the shooting was justified while a civil jury later found two of the four officers grossly negligent for the same conduct?
What specific tactical planning, if any, accounted for the possibility of bystanders — including a known infant — in the vehicle before officers opened fire?
What changes, if any, did the Virginia Beach Police Department make to its SWAT engagement protocols as a result of this case?
