name: Jayland Walker
summary: Jayland Walker, 25, was shot and killed by eight Akron, Ohio police officers on June 27, 2022, after fleeing a traffic stop for a broken taillight, firing a single shot from his car during the pursuit, then exiting and running on foot. Police said Walker, who was unarmed when he was shot, made a motion officers interpreted as reaching for a weapon; a gun was later found in his abandoned vehicle. The eight officers fired 94 shots in 6.7 seconds, striking Walker with 46 entrance or graze wounds, including several in the back, according to the county medical examiner. A special grand jury seated by Ohio's attorney general declined to indict any of the officers in April 2023, finding their use of force legally justified. The city later paid Walker's family a $4.8 million settlement. No one has ever been criminally charged in Walker's death.
known: The traffic stop, chase, and shooting, per Akron Police Department body camera footage released publicly and the Summit County Medical Examiner's autopsy findings.
Walker fired one shot from his vehicle during the car chase, according to police; a gun was later recovered from his abandoned car, and shell casings recovered at the scene matched it.
Walker was unarmed at the moment the eight officers opened fire on him after the foot chase.
The Summit County Medical Examiner found Walker suffered 46 entrance or graze wounds from the 94 total shots fired, with no drugs or alcohol in his system.

A special nine-member grand jury — three men, six women, two of them Black — reviewed more than 100 interviews and over 50 body-camera videos before declining to indict any of the eight officers on April 17, 2023, per Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost.

The City of Akron settled a federal wrongful death and civil rights lawsuit with Walker's family for $4.8 million, and changed its vehicle-pursuit policy to bar chases over equipment violations alone.
unknown: Whether Walker's motion toward his waistband while running — the act officers cited as justifying deadly force — constituted an actual threat, given he was in fact unarmed at that moment, was never tested at any criminal trial.
The specific vote count of the special grand jury has never been made public, as Ohio law precludes disclosure of grand jury deliberations.
Why officers continued firing across the full 6.7-second span, including shots that struck Walker in the back, has not been individually addressed for each of the eight officers involved.
unanswered: Why did 94 shots fired by eight officers in under seven seconds, striking an unarmed man 46 times, meet the legal standard for justified use of force?
What specific evidence led the grand jury to its conclusion, given the proceedings themselves remain legally sealed?
What further reforms, beyond the pursuit policy change, has Akron made to its use-of-force training as a direct result of this case?

name: Ta'Kiya Young
summary: Ta'Kiya Young, 21, seven months pregnant with her third child, was shot and killed by Blendon Township, Ohio Police Officer Connor Grubb on August 24, 2023, in a Kroger parking lot after being accused of shoplifting alcohol. Body camera footage showed Grubb standing in front of Young's car as she slowly rolled it forward attempting to leave; he fired a single shot through the windshield, killing her and her unborn daughter. A Franklin County grand jury indicted Grubb on murder, felonious assault, and involuntary manslaughter charges in August 2024, a year after the shooting. On November 21, 2025, following a roughly two-week trial, a jury acquitted Grubb of all six charges after about 6.5 hours of deliberation, finding his use of force objectively reasonable given the moving vehicle. No one has ever been convicted in Young's death.
known: The shoplifting accusation, the parking lot confrontation, and the single fatal shot, per body camera footage played at trial and the Franklin County grand jury's charging documents.

Grubb fired one shot through the windshield as Young's car rolled forward and made contact with him; the judge later dismissed four charges specifically tied to the death of Young's unborn daughter, ruling prosecutors had not proven Grubb knew she was pregnant.
A Franklin County grand jury indicted Grubb in August 2024, a year after the shooting, on two counts each of murder, felonious assault, and involuntary manslaughter.

At trial, the defense argued the slow-moving vehicle itself constituted deadly force, citing testimony from a use-of-force expert and an accident reconstructionist; prosecutors argued Young posed no threat justifying deadly force.
A jury acquitted Grubb of all six charges on November 21, 2025, after about 6.5 hours of deliberation.
Young's estate filed a civil lawsuit against Blendon Township and its police chief over department practices, which remains pending following the acquittal.

Whether Grubb was aware of Young's pregnancy at the time he fired has never been established either way; the court found prosecutors did not prove that he was.
The jury's specific reasoning across six separate charges and roughly 6.5 hours of deliberation is not public, as with all jury deliberations.
unanswered: Why did it take a full year after the shooting for a grand jury to indict Grubb, and what specifically changed in that year?
What became of Young's estate's civil lawsuit against Blendon Township and its police chief following the criminal acquittal?
What department-wide policy changes, if any, has Blendon Township made regarding responses to suspected shoplifting since this case?

name: Patrick Lyoya
summary: Patrick Lyoya, 26, a Congolese refugee, was shot in the back of the head by Grand Rapids, Michigan Police Officer Christopher Schurr during a traffic stop on April 4, 2022. Lyoya ran after Schurr pulled him over for a mismatched license plate; Schurr caught him, and the two struggled over Schurr's Taser for roughly two and a half minutes before Schurr, straddling Lyoya face-down on the ground, fired a single shot into the back of his head. Schurr was fired and charged with second-degree murder in June 2022, becoming one of the few Michigan officers ever criminally charged for an on-duty killing. After a three-year legal battle, his trial began in April 2025; a jury deliberated over 20 hours across four days before deadlocking, and a mistrial was declared on May 8, 2025. Kent County's prosecutor announced on May 22, 2025 that he would not seek a retrial, concluding a second trial was unlikely to produce a different result. No one has ever been convicted in Lyoya's death.
known: The traffic stop, the roughly two-and-a-half-minute struggle over the Taser, and the fatal shot, per body camera, dashcam, and bystander cellphone video released by the Grand Rapids Police Department.
Schurr was on top of Lyoya, who was face-down on the ground, when he fired the single fatal shot to the back of Lyoya's head.
Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker charged Schurr with second-degree murder in June 2022; Schurr was fired from the department the same month.
Lyoya's autopsy showed a blood alcohol content more than three times the legal driving limit, and a witness testified he had been drinking the day before his death.

The jury of 14 (12 regular jurors plus two alternates), predominantly white, deliberated more than 20 hours over four days before telling the court it was deadlocked; Judge Christina Mims declared a mistrial on May 8, 2025.
Prosecutor Becker announced on May 22, 2025 that he would not seek a retrial, stating he did not believe a second trial would produce a different verdict.
A separate federal civil rights lawsuit against Schurr and the city remains active; a judge denied Schurr's motion to dismiss it, and a jury trial was scheduled for October 2026.

Whether Lyoya, face-down on the ground with Schurr on top of him, still posed the "jeopardy" to Schurr that the defense argued justified deadly force was disputed by the prosecution and never resolved by any verdict.

Why did the prosecutor conclude a retrial was unlikely to produce a different result, and what specific factors from the first trial led to that assessment?
What will the pending federal civil rights trial, scheduled for October 2026, add to the public record that the criminal trial did not resolve?

name: Rayshard Brooks
summary: Rayshard Brooks, 27, was shot and killed by Atlanta Police Officer Garrett Rolfe outside a Wendy's restaurant on June 12, 2020, after a struggle that began when officers tried to arrest him for driving under the influence. Brooks resisted, grabbed a Taser from Officer Devin Brosnan, and ran; an autopsy found he was shot twice in the back. Then-Fulton County District Attorney Paul Howard charged Rolfe with felony murder within days, less than three weeks after George Floyd's killing sparked nationwide protests. Howard lost his re-election bid months later, and the case was passed between three successive prosecutors before a special prosecutor appointed by Georgia's attorney general dismissed all charges against both officers in August 2022, finding the shooting objectively reasonable. Rolfe, initially fired, was reinstated with back pay by the city's Civil Service Board. No one has ever been convicted in Brooks's death.
known: The DUI stop, the struggle, and the shooting, per Atlanta Police Department body and dash camera footage released publicly.
Brooks grabbed a Taser from Officer Brosnan during the struggle and fired it at Rolfe while fleeing; Rolfe fired three shots, striking Brooks twice in the back, per the autopsy.
Fulton County District Attorney Paul Howard charged Rolfe with felony murder and other counts, and Brosnan with aggravated assault, within five days of the shooting.
The Atlanta Civil Service Board reinstated Rolfe with back pay in May 2021, finding the city had denied him due process in his firing.

Special prosecutor Peter Skandalakis, appointed by the Georgia attorney general after Howard lost re-election, announced in August 2022 — more than two years after the shooting — that both officers "committed no crimes" and dismissed all charges, finding the use of force objectively reasonable given Brooks firing the Taser at Rolfe as he fled.
Brooks's family filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the City of Atlanta in September 2021, which remained active following the dismissal of criminal charges.
unknown: Whether firing a Taser — a less-lethal weapon — while fleeing justified a fatal shooting that struck Brooks twice in the back has never been tested at any criminal trial, since the case never reached one.

Whether the original charges were, as the officers' attorneys and some commentators argued, rushed for political reasons by a district attorney facing re-election, or were withdrawn for political reasons under a differently pressured process two years later, has been argued from both directions and never independently resolved.

The specific evidentiary basis Skandalakis weighed differently from Howard's original charging decision, given both reviewed largely the same body camera footage, was not fully detailed in his public announcement.
unanswered: Why did the criminal case take more than two years and three different prosecutors to reach a final decision?
What became of Brooks's family's wrongful death lawsuit against the City of Atlanta?
What specific factors led the Atlanta Civil Service Board to find Rolfe's firing violated his due process rights, and did that finding affect the later charging decision?

name: Amir Locke
summary: Amir Locke, 22, an aspiring hip-hop artist, was shot and killed by Minneapolis Police SWAT Officer Mark Hanneman on February 2, 2022, within about ten seconds of officers using a key to enter his cousin's apartment on a no-knock warrant tied to a homicide investigation in neighboring St. Paul. Locke, asleep on the couch under a blanket, was not named in the warrant and was not a suspect in the investigation. Body camera video showed him stirring awake and rising with a handgun he was legally licensed to carry as officers shouted commands; Hanneman shot him three times, saying Locke had pointed the gun toward officers, a characterization Locke's family disputed. Minnesota's attorney general and the Hennepin County attorney jointly announced in April 2022 that there was insufficient evidence to charge Hanneman. No one has ever been charged in Locke's death.
known: The no-knock entry, the roughly ten-second span between entry and gunfire, and the shooting, per Minneapolis Police Department body camera footage released publicly.
Locke was not named on the search warrant and was not a suspect in the St. Paul homicide investigation the warrant related to.
Locke held a valid Minnesota permit to carry the handgun found in his hand.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and Hennepin County Attorney Michael Freeman jointly announced on April 6, 2022 that there was insufficient admissible evidence to disprove beyond a reasonable doubt that Hanneman's use of force was legally authorized, and declined to charge him.

Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey ordered an immediate moratorium on no-knock warrants days after the shooting and later formalized a policy requiring officers to knock and announce before entering in most circumstances.
Locke's family filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the city and Hanneman in February 2023, one year after his death.
unknown: Whether Locke in fact pointed the handgun toward officers, as Hanneman's account maintained and prosecutors found sufficient to preclude charges, or whether he was simply startled awake and reaching for a legally owned weapon without directing it at anyone, as his family argued from the same body camera footage, was never resolved by any criminal trial.

Why Locke, asleep and not named in the warrant, was in the apartment at the specific moment of the raid has been explained by the family as simply staying at his cousin's home, though this was not centrally addressed in the prosecutors' charging decision.
The full internal SWAT team briefing materials for the raid, including what officers were told about who might be present in the apartment, have not been made comprehensively public.
unanswered: Why did officers have only about ten seconds between entry and the fatal shot to assess whether an unnamed, sleeping occupant posed a threat?
What specifically distinguished this case from Breonna Taylor's, given both involved no-knock warrants and both resulted in no charges against the officer who fired the fatal shots?
What became of the Locke family's federal civil rights lawsuit against the city and Officer Hanneman?

name: Andrew Brown Jr.
summary: Andrew Brown Jr., 42, a father of seven, was shot and killed by Pasquotank County, North Carolina sheriff's deputies on April 21, 2021, while sitting in his car as they attempted to serve felony drug arrest and search warrants at his home in Elizabeth City. Three of the seven deputies present fired 14 shots as Brown's car pulled away; he was killed by a shot to the back of the head. He was unarmed, and no weapon was found in his vehicle. District Attorney Andrew Womble announced on May 18, 2021 — the day after a jury convicted Derek Chauvin of murdering George Floyd — that the shooting was "justified" because Brown's car had made contact with a deputy, and declined to bring any charges. Brown's family, reviewing the same body camera footage, said he never posed a threat and was "executed" while trying to drive away. No one has ever been charged in Brown's death.
known: The warrant service, the shooting, and Brown's death from a shot to the back of the head, per the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation's inquiry and District Attorney Andrew Womble's public presentation of body camera footage.
Deputies fired a total of 14 shots from two handguns and a rifle; three of the seven deputies present fired, while four did not.
No weapon was found in Brown's vehicle.

District Attorney Womble announced on May 18, 2021 that the shooting was justified because Brown's vehicle made contact with a deputy as he attempted to drive away, and that no charges would be filed against any of the deputies.
Brown's family, after viewing body camera and dashcam footage, disputed Womble's account, saying deputies fired from a sidewalk at a car that was moving away from them and posed no threat.

Brown's family filed a federal wrongful death lawsuit in July 2021; the killing also prompted the NAACP to request a Department of Justice pattern-or-practice investigation into the Pasquotank Sheriff's Office and Womble's office.
unknown: Whether Brown's vehicle in fact struck a deputy in a manner presenting a deadly threat, as Womble concluded, or whether the car was simply moving away with no one in its path, as the family's review of the same footage maintained, was never tested at any criminal trial.
Why four of the seven deputies present chose not to fire, if the threat was as immediate as Womble's justification implied, has not been addressed in any official public accounting.

The full, unredacted body camera footage was only released to the public in edited form with faces obscured, per a court order, limiting independent public review of the moments immediately following the shooting.
unanswered: Why did four of the seven deputies present not fire their weapons if Brown's vehicle posed the deadly threat that justified deadly force?
Did the Department of Justice ever open the pattern-or-practice investigation the NAACP and other advocates requested into the Pasquotank Sheriff's Office?
What became of Brown's family's federal wrongful death lawsuit?

name: Aiyana Stanley-Jones
summary: Aiyana Stanley-Jones, 7, was shot in the head and killed by Detroit Police Special Response Team Officer Joseph Weekley just after midnight on May 16, 2010, as she slept on a couch next to her grandmother during a raid on their home in search of a murder suspect who did not live there. The raid, being filmed for the A&E reality show "The First 48," began with another officer throwing a flash-bang grenade through the window; Weekley, first through the door, said his gun fired when the girl's grandmother, Mertilla Jones, struck it during a struggle, which she denied under oath. Weekley was charged with involuntary manslaughter and careless discharge of a firearm. His first trial ended in a hung jury in 2013; a judge later dismissed the manslaughter charge outright during his second trial in 2014, and that jury deadlocked on the remaining misdemeanor count as well, resulting in a second mistrial. Prosecutors declined to pursue a third trial, and all charges were formally dropped in January 2015. No one has ever been convicted in Aiyana's death.
known: The raid, the flash-bang grenade, and the shooting, per Detroit Police Department records and trial testimony from both of Weekley's criminal trials.
The raid was being filmed for the A&E reality television series "The First 48"; Aiyana's family has said they believe officers' conduct that night was influenced by the presence of cameras.

Weekley testified his gun discharged when Mertilla Jones, Aiyana's grandmother, struck it during a struggle; Jones testified under oath that she never touched the weapon, and another officer present testified there was no struggle.

Weekley's first trial in 2013 ended in a hung jury; in his 2014 retrial, the judge dismissed the involuntary manslaughter charge for insufficient evidence, and the remaining jury deadlocked on the misdemeanor careless-discharge charge, resulting in a second mistrial.
Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy announced in January 2015 that her office would not seek a third trial, and all charges against Weekley were formally dismissed.

The actual murder suspect police were searching for did not live at the address raided and was apprehended elsewhere; Aiyana's father was separately convicted of providing that suspect with the murder weapon in an unrelated case.
unknown: Whether Weekley's gun discharged because Jones struck it, as he maintained, or accidentally for another reason, as Jones and a fellow officer's testimony suggested, was never resolved — two separate juries could not agree.
Why officers conducted the raid on the wrong address for the suspect they sought has not been fully explained in public reporting beyond acknowledgment that the raid targeted the wrong home.
The extent to which the presence of reality television cameras affected officers' tactical decisions that night, as the family has alleged, has never been independently investigated or resolved.
unanswered: Why did police raid a home where the actual suspect did not live, and what accountability existed for that underlying error separate from the shooting itself?

Did the presence of "The First 48" film crew affect how the raid was planned or executed, and has any police department policy changed regarding embedded media on tactical raids as a result of this case?
What became of Aiyana's family's civil lawsuit against the city of Detroit following the criminal charges being dropped?

name: Aura Rosser
summary: Aura Rosser, 40, an artist and mother of three who was living with addiction, was shot and killed by Ann Arbor, Michigan Police Officer David Ried in her home in the early morning hours of November 10, 2014, within five to ten seconds of officers entering the house. Her boyfriend, Victor Stephens, had called police to report a domestic dispute and asked them to remove Rosser from the home, but said afterward that lethal force was not justified. Police said Rosser approached officers with a knife; Officer Mark Raab fired a Taser at the same moment Ried fired his handgun, striking her once in the chest. The Washtenaw County Prosecutor's Office declined to charge Ried in January 2015, finding the shooting lawful self-defense. No one has ever been charged in Rosser's death.
known: The domestic violence call, the officers' entry, and the shooting within five to ten seconds of entry, per the Washtenaw County Prosecutor's report following a two-month Michigan State Police investigation.
Officer Raab discharged his Taser at the same moment Officer Ried fired his handgun; Rosser was struck once in the chest and pronounced dead at the scene.
Rosser's boyfriend, Victor Stephens, who made the 911 call, said afterward that he wanted police to remove Rosser from the house but did not believe lethal force was justified.
Washtenaw County Prosecutor Brian Mackie announced on January 30, 2015 that Ried would not be charged, concluding he acted in lawful self-defense.
Ann Arbor Police Chief John Baird later wrote in an internal memo that the shooting was "justified by any legal, policy or reasonable moral standard," while also calling it "incredibly tragic."

In response to Rosser's death, Ann Arbor's City Council passed a resolution in December 2014 to implement body cameras for the police department, and the shooting prompted years of sustained local organizing under the name "Ann Arbor to Ferguson."
unknown: Whether Rosser's approach with the knife, in the five to ten seconds after officers entered an unfamiliar situation at night, presented the kind of imminent threat that justified lethal force was never tested at any criminal trial.

Full, unedited body camera or dashcam footage of the shooting itself was not available at the time, since the department had not yet adopted body cameras — a gap the shooting itself prompted the city to address going forward.

Whether responding officers had any advance information about Rosser's mental health or substance use history, and whether that would have changed their approach, has not been detailed in public reporting.
unanswered: Why did officers not attempt a non-lethal option exclusively, given a Taser was already being deployed by a second officer at the same moment the fatal shot was fired?
What specific training in de-escalating domestic violence and mental health crisis calls did the responding officers have at the time, and did that training change afterward?
What tangible outcomes did the sustained "Ann Arbor to Ferguson" organizing effort achieve in the years following Rosser's death?

name: Terrance Kellom
summary: Terrance Kellom, 20, was shot and killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Officer Mitchell Quinn on April 27, 2015, at his father's Detroit home, in front of his family, as a multi-agency federal fugitive task force served an arrest warrant on an armed-robbery charge. Quinn said Kellom, who had hidden in an attic, dropped down and lunged at him with a hammer, forcing him to fire; Kellom's father maintained his son died with clenched fists and no hammer. Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy declined to charge Quinn in August 2015, citing blood-spatter evidence she said supported his account. Nearly four years later, during sworn deposition testimony in the family's federal lawsuit, a Detroit police officer who had witnessed the shooting and originally corroborated the hammer account testified he could no longer recall seeing a hammer at all. No one has ever been charged in Kellom's death.
known: The federal task force raid, the shooting inside the home, and Kellom's death in front of family members, per the Wayne County Prosecutor's public findings and subsequent federal civil litigation.

Prosecutor Kym Worthy announced on August 19, 2015 that the shooting was justified by self-defense and the defense of others, citing blood-spatter patterns she said showed Kellom continued advancing after being shot.

In a November 2018 deposition connected to the family's federal wrongful death lawsuit, Detroit Police Officer Darrel Fitzgerald — who had written two days after the shooting that he saw Kellom raise a hammer above his shoulder — testified he could not recall seeing any hammer and instead recalled Kellom on his knees rather than advancing.

The family's attorney also cited the absence of Kellom's fingerprints on the recovered hammer, inconsistent shell casing evidence he said could indicate more than one shooter, and a lack of evidence photographs.

Following the deposition, civil rights attorneys and Kellom's family publicly called for Michigan's attorney general to reopen the case; the federal government disputed that Fitzgerald's testimony constituted a genuine recantation.

Quinn had a documented prior history, including a 2000 lawsuit settled by the city over an earlier false arrest allegation and 2008 domestic violence-related charges against him that were later dropped for insufficient evidence; he joined ICE months after those charges were dropped.
unknown: Whether Kellom in fact held and raised a hammer, as Quinn maintained and the original prosecutorial review found supported by the evidence, or whether he was unarmed and on his knees, as a witnessing officer's later sworn testimony suggested, has never been resolved in any criminal proceeding.
Why fingerprint evidence did not connect Kellom to the hammer despite blood matching him being found on it has not been fully explained in public reporting.

Whether Michigan's attorney general's office, which said in 2019 it would review the case following the deposition, reached any further conclusion has not been consistently reported in available public sources.
unanswered: Why did a key witnessing officer's sworn account of the central physical evidence — whether Kellom held a hammer at all — change so significantly between his original written report and his later deposition testimony?
Why were no fingerprints from Kellom found on the hammer despite it reportedly bearing his blood?
Did Michigan's attorney general's office ever complete and publicly release the findings of the review it agreed to conduct following the 2019 deposition revelations?

name: Kendrec McDade
summary: Kendrec McDade, 19, a college student, was shot seven times and killed by Pasadena, California Police Officers Jeffrey Newlen and Matthew Griffin on March 24, 2012, after they chased him down a residential street responding to a 911 call describing an armed robbery. The caller, Oscar Carrillo, had lied about the robbers being armed and mentioned a gun eight times to get a faster police response; his backpack had in fact been stolen from his car in an unarmed burglary. McDade, who was unarmed, was shot while reportedly reaching toward his waistband as he ran. He was left handcuffed on the ground for roughly eight minutes before paramedics arrived, his last words reportedly "Why did they shoot me?" The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office cleared both officers of criminal wrongdoing in December 2012, finding they acted in lawful self-defense. Carrillo separately pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor counts of filing a false police report, receiving 90 days in jail — the only criminal conviction connected to the case. No officer has ever been charged in McDade's death.
known: The false 911 call, the chase, and the shooting, per the Pasadena Police Department, the LA County District Attorney's charge evaluation, and Carrillo's own admissions.
Carrillo admitted he lied about the robbers being armed, mentioning a gun eight times during the 911 call, to get police to respond faster; no gun or stolen merchandise was ever found on McDade.
McDade was shot seven times, per the autopsy, and was left handcuffed on the ground for roughly eight minutes before receiving medical attention, according to his family's attorney.

The LA County District Attorney's Office announced in December 2012, after an eight-month investigation, that officers Newlen and Griffin acted in lawful self-defense and would not be charged, concluding McDade's motion toward his waistband was consistent with reaching for a firearm.

Oscar Carrillo pleaded guilty in 2013 to two misdemeanor counts of filing a false police report, receiving a 90-day jail sentence, 90 days of community service, and a $3,000 fine payable to the Pasadena Police Department; prosecutors had declined to charge him with involuntary manslaughter.
McDade's parents separately settled federal civil rights lawsuits against the City of Pasadena in 2014, with settlement amounts not publicly disclosed.
unknown: Whether McDade's motion toward his waistband while running away actually resembled reaching for a weapon, as officers maintained, or was an ambiguous gesture given he had no weapon at all, was disputed by the family's attorney, who characterized "waistband shootings" as a recurring pattern in the region, and was never tested at a criminal trial.
Why officers did not provide first aid during the roughly eight minutes McDade was handcuffed and reportedly still speaking has not been fully addressed in any official public accounting.
The scene was in a dark, mixed-use area with no independent civilian witnesses, per police, meaning the officers' own accounts formed the primary basis for the self-defense finding.
unanswered: Why was the only criminal conviction in this case a misdemeanor false-report charge against the 911 caller, while the officers who fired the fatal shots faced no charges at all?
What specifically occurred in the roughly eight minutes between the shooting and paramedics' arrival, and why was no first aid provided during that window?
What became of the broader pattern the family's attorney alleged regarding other "waistband shooting" cases in the Los Angeles area?

name: Miles Hall
summary: Miles Hall, 23, who had schizophrenia, was shot four times and killed by Walnut Creek, California Police Officers KC Hsiao and Melissa Murphy on June 2, 2019, during a mental health crisis near his home. His mother, Taun Hall, had called and left a voicemail with a Walnut Creek officer the day before, warning that her son was having "another episode" and asking them to be prepared. When officers responded to reports Hall was carrying a nearly 5-foot steel digging tool and had chased a vehicle on foot, they deployed a beanbag shotgun first; when that failed to stop him, Hsiao and Murphy shot him. The Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office announced in May 2021, nearly two years later, that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute either officer. No one has ever been charged in Hall's death.
known: Taun Hall's voicemail to a Walnut Creek police officer the day before the shooting, warning that her son was experiencing another mental health episode, per a transcript reported by local media.
Witnesses reported Hall was carrying a nearly 5-foot-long steel digging tool and had chased at least one vehicle on foot before officers arrived and staged roughly ten minutes later.
Officers first deployed a beanbag shotgun, which did not stop Hall; Officers Hsiao and Murphy then shot him a combined four times.

Contra Costa County District Attorney Diana Becton's office announced on May 7, 2021 that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute either officer, citing the officers' self-defense claim and danger to the surrounding neighborhood.

In September 2021, the City of Walnut Creek approved a $4 million settlement with Hall's family in a related civil rights lawsuit; the family used part of the settlement to establish the Miles Hall Foundation, focused on reforming law enforcement responses to mental health crises.
Following the shooting, Walnut Creek expanded funding for mobile mental health crisis units as an alternative to police response for such calls.
unknown: Whether officers had, as Hall's mother stated, arrived with an established plan for de-escalating a mental health crisis specific to her son, and whether that plan was followed, was disputed by the family's attorney and never resolved by any criminal proceeding.

Whether nonlethal options beyond the single beanbag shotgun deployment were reasonably available before officers resorted to gunfire has been disputed by the family but was not independently tested at trial.
Why the district attorney's charging decision took nearly two years to reach has not been fully explained in public reporting.
unanswered: Given that Hall's own mother had proactively warned police the day before about his mental health crisis, why did the department's response still end in a fatal shooting?
Why did the district attorney's charging review take nearly two years, and what specifically was under investigation for that length of time?
What measurable outcomes has the Miles Hall Foundation's advocacy work achieved in changing how other departments respond to mental health crisis calls?

name: Jonathan Sanders
summary: Jonathan Sanders, 39, a horse trainer, died on July 8, 2015 in Stonewall, Mississippi after an encounter with police officer Kevin Herrington that witnesses said involved a chokehold lasting as long as 20 to 30 minutes. Sanders had been riding a horse-drawn buggy near a gas station when he intervened in an argument between Herrington and another man he knew; witnesses said Herrington's patrol lights startled Sanders's horse, throwing him to the ground, after which Herrington grabbed him and restrained him on the ground. Multiple witnesses told the family's attorneys Herrington said he was "going to get that [racial slur]" before the confrontation and that Sanders repeatedly said "I can't breathe" before he died at the scene. A grand jury declined to indict Herrington in January 2016, and a second grand jury concluded in March 2016 that Sanders had choked to death after swallowing cocaine he was trying to hide, finding no excessive force was used. No one has ever been charged in Sanders's death.
known: The confrontation, the restraint, and Sanders's death at the scene, per the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation's inquiry and multiple witness accounts relayed by the family's attorneys.

Multiple witnesses told the family's attorneys, Chokwe Antar Lumumba and C.J. Lawrence, that Herrington restrained Sanders on the ground for an extended period, with estimates from witnesses ranging up to 20 to 30 minutes; the attorneys themselves noted witness time estimates under stress are often inflated.
At least one witness reported hearing Herrington say he was "going to get that [racial slur]" in reference to Sanders before the physical confrontation began.
A witness who offered to retrieve a breathing mask to help Sanders said Herrington refused the offer; witnesses also reported hearing Sanders repeat "I can't breathe."

A grand jury declined to indict Herrington on any charge in January 2016; a second grand jury review in March 2016 concluded Sanders died of asphyxiation from "acute cocaine toxicity" after swallowing cocaine, and found police had not used excessive force in restraining him.
Herrington claimed Sanders reached for his service weapon during the struggle, a claim witnesses disputed.
unknown: Whether Sanders's death was caused primarily by asphyxiation from restraint, as multiple eyewitnesses' accounts suggested, or from cocaine toxicity as the grand jury concluded, was disputed by the family's attorneys, who said a preliminary autopsy review pointed to manual strangulation, and has never been resolved by any criminal trial.
Whether Herrington in fact used a racial slur before the encounter, as multiple witnesses told the family's attorneys, was never independently adjudicated.
The exact duration Sanders was restrained — estimated by different witnesses from several minutes up to 30 — was never precisely established.
unanswered: Why did the second grand jury's cocaine-toxicity finding differ so sharply from multiple eyewitness accounts describing a prolonged chokehold and Sanders saying he could not breathe?
Was the witness account describing Herrington's use of a racial slur before the encounter ever formally investigated as evidence of intent?
Why was a witness's offer to provide a breathing mask allegedly refused, and was that refusal examined in either grand jury proceeding?

name: Tyre King
summary: Tyre King, 13, was shot and killed by Columbus, Ohio Police Officer Bryan Mason on September 14, 2016, during a foot chase after officers responded to a report of an armed $10 robbery. Mason said King pulled a BB gun with an attached laser sight from his waistband during the chase, prompting him to fire; an older teenager who had been with King, Demetrious Braxton, later told the Columbus Dispatch that King was running away, not reaching for anything, when he was shot. A Franklin County grand jury declined to indict Mason — who had been involved in three prior fatal or use-of-force shootings before this one — in May 2017. A federal jury separately cleared Mason of civil liability in 2023, after the judge excluded testimony about Mason's history of 47 use-of-force reports in the seven years preceding King's death. No one has ever been charged in King's death.
known: The robbery report, the foot chase, and the shooting, per the Columbus Division of Police and Franklin County Prosecutor Ron O'Brien's public account following the grand jury proceedings.
A BB gun with an attached laser sight, with the orange safety tip that typically distinguishes replica firearms not visible or removed, was recovered at the scene.
Demetrious Braxton, the 19-year-old who had been with King and later pleaded guilty to the underlying robbery charge, told reporters King was running, not pulling out the BB gun, when he was shot.

Officer Mason had been involved in three previous police shootings before King's death, including a 2012 fatal shooting for which he was cleared, and had accumulated 47 use-of-force reports in the seven years prior, per Columbus Dispatch reporting.
A Franklin County grand jury, after a two-day proceeding involving 15 to 17 witnesses, declined to indict Mason on May 19, 2017.

King's grandmother filed a federal civil rights lawsuit in 2018; a federal jury found in January 2023 that Mason did not violate King's constitutional rights, after the judge excluded testimony from a police practices expert about Mason's use-of-force history from being presented to that jury.
unknown: Whether King was in fact reaching for the BB gun, as Mason maintained, or was simply running away, as a fellow teenager present that night stated, was disputed and never resolved by either the grand jury or the later federal civil trial.

The full extent of what Mason's 47 prior use-of-force reports and three earlier shootings might have shown about a pattern in his conduct was not presented to the federal civil jury, since the judge excluded that evidence.

Whether cover and concealment were reasonably available to Mason before he resorted to deadly force, as the family's use-of-force expert argued in written testimony the court did not allow him to deliver live, was never weighed by any jury.
unanswered: Why was expert testimony about Mason's extensive prior use-of-force history excluded from the federal civil trial, and how might its inclusion have changed the outcome?
Why did Mason remain an active-duty officer, later moved only to narcotics duty, despite three previous shootings before King's death?
What specific parallels and differences exist between this case and Tamir Rice's, given how frequently the two were compared in contemporaneous coverage?

name: John Neville
summary: John Neville, 56, died on December 4, 2019, three days after Forsyth County, North Carolina jail detention officers restrained him face-down on the floor of his cell in a "bent-leg prone restraint" for nearly an hour. Body camera video showed Neville, who had fallen from his top bunk during an apparent seizure, saying "I can't breathe" and calling out for his deceased mother more than 25 times while restrained; officers responded at least twice with "if you can talk, you can breathe." A medical examiner ruled the death a homicide from positional and compressional asphyxia. Five detention officers and a jail nurse were charged with involuntary manslaughter in 2020; a grand jury declined to indict any of the five officers in April 2022, indicting only the nurse, Michelle Heughins — whose attorney argued she was the only person present who tried to save Neville's life. In 2023, at the Neville family's own request, prosecutors dropped the remaining charge against Heughins as well. No one has ever been convicted in Neville's death.
known: The restraint, the nearly hour-long prone position, and Neville's death three days later, per body camera video released by court order and the county medical examiner's autopsy finding of homicide by positional and compressional asphyxia.

Neville said "I can't breathe" and called out for his mother repeatedly — accounts range from at least 10 to more than 25 times across different reporting — while restrained; officers are recorded responding that if he could talk, he could breathe.
Five detention officers and jail nurse Michelle Heughins were charged with involuntary manslaughter in July 2020, following a seven-month investigation.
A Forsyth County grand jury declined in April 2022 to indict any of the five officers, indicting only Heughins on the involuntary manslaughter charge.

In September 2023, prosecutors dropped the remaining charge against Heughins specifically at the request of Neville's family, who by then had expressed disappointment that the sole person charged was the nurse rather than any of the restraining officers.
The Forsyth County Sheriff's Office banned the "bent-leg prone restraint" technique used on Neville in August 2020, and the county settled a related civil claim with Neville's family for $3 million.
The sheriff's office did not publicly acknowledge Neville's death for roughly six to seven months, only providing information after inquiries from the Winston-Salem Journal.
unknown: Why the grand jury indicted only the nurse — whose attorney and Neville's own son both publicly said the evidence showed responsibility was shared far more broadly — while clearing all five officers who physically restrained him, has never been explained in any public grand jury record, which remains sealed by law.

The full extent of what jail policy, cited by Heughins's defense as limiting her ability to intervene, actually constrained her actions in the room has been disputed between her attorney's account and the family's.
Why the sheriff's office waited six to seven months to publicly acknowledge Neville's death has not been fully resolved beyond the sheriff's stated reliance on the family's initial wishes.
unanswered: Why did the grand jury single out the jail nurse for indictment while clearing all five officers who physically restrained Neville for nearly an hour?
What jail policies, if any, genuinely limited Nurse Heughins's ability to intervene sooner, and were those policies themselves ever examined for liability?
What became of the Neville family's pending federal civil lawsuit against Forsyth County, the sheriff, and Wellpath, the jail's former medical provider?

name: Ronald Greene
summary: Ronald Greene, 49, died on May 10, 2019, following a high-speed chase and arrest by Louisiana State Police troopers outside Monroe, Louisiana. Authorities initially told his family he died from injuries sustained when his car crashed at the end of the chase. Body camera video, suppressed for two years until an Associated Press investigation obtained and published it in 2021, instead showed troopers stunning Greene with Tasers, punching him, and dragging him by his ankle shackles face-down on the ground while he pleaded, "I'm scared! I'm your brother!" Five officers were eventually indicted in 2022 on charges ranging from negligent homicide to malfeasance. By 2024, prosecutors had dropped the most serious charges against every defendant; the lead trooper avoided trial entirely by pleading no contest to a single misdemeanor battery charge in exchange for probation. The Department of Justice separately declined to bring federal charges. No one has ever been convicted of a felony in Greene's death.
known: The high-speed chase, the arrest, and Greene's death, per body camera video an Associated Press investigation obtained and published in 2021, two years after Louisiana State Police initially attributed his death to the car crash alone.

The video showed troopers using stun guns on Greene, punching him, and dragging him face-down by his ankle shackles while he begged for mercy; a state police force instructor who reviewed the footage described the troopers' conduct as "torture and murder," per multiple news reports.

State police records showed a coroner's report listed the cause of death as a motor vehicle accident, a state crash report omitted any mention of troopers using force, and 462 days passed before state police even opened an internal investigation.
Five Louisiana officers, including four state troopers and one Union Parish sheriff's deputy, were indicted in December 2022 on charges ranging from negligent homicide to malfeasance in office.

By September 2024, prosecutors had dismissed the negligent homicide charge against the trooper most directly implicated in Greene's death, Kory York, leaving only lesser malfeasance counts against two remaining defendants.

In October 2024, York avoided trial entirely by pleading no contest to a single misdemeanor battery charge, receiving one year of probation and no jail time, in exchange for agreeing to testify against the one officer still facing charges; Greene's mother said the family had refused to sign the plea deal and were not consulted on its final terms.

The U.S. Department of Justice, after opening a broader civil rights investigation into Louisiana State Police, told Greene's family in 2024 that it would not bring federal criminal charges in his death specifically.
One indicted trooper, Chris Hollingsworth, died in a single-vehicle crash in September 2020, hours after learning he would be fired for his role in Greene's death.
unknown: The precise physical cause of Greene's death was never conclusively established by prosecutors despite years of investigation, which CBS News reported was itself cited as a weakness that discouraged more serious charges.

Why state police and the coroner's office initially attributed Greene's death solely to the car crash, despite injuries an emergency room doctor reportedly questioned at the time, has never been fully accounted for by any single official investigation.
The full extent of what Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards knew about the case and when, which a state legislative inquiry examined, was not conclusively resolved in public reporting.
unanswered: Why did it take 462 days for Louisiana State Police to open even an internal investigation into a death captured on body camera video?
Why was the case's most serious charge, negligent homicide, ultimately reduced to a single misdemeanor with no jail time for the trooper most directly involved?
What specific findings, if any, has the Department of Justice's broader pattern-or-practice investigation into Louisiana State Police produced regarding the treatment of Black motorists?

CBS News — “Louisiana prosecutors drop most serious charge in fatal arrest of Black motorist Ronald Greene”

name: Alonzo Smith
summary: Alonzo Smith, 27, died on November 1, 2015 after being restrained and handcuffed by two privately employed "special police officers" at Marbury Plaza apartments in Southeast Washington, D.C. Neighbors reported hearing Smith, who was shirtless and barefoot, running and screaming that someone was trying to kill him before the special officers caught him, put him in a bear hug, and held him face-down on the ground. When Metropolitan Police arrived, Smith was found handcuffed, unconscious, and not breathing; he died at a hospital soon after. The D.C. medical examiner classified his death a homicide. Nearly a year later, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced there was insufficient evidence to charge either special officer, attributing Smith's death to a cocaine-related cardiac event that restraint may have contributed to, rather than to excessive force. No one has ever been charged in Smith's death, and the special officers involved have never been publicly identified.
known: The restraint, the discovery of Smith handcuffed and not breathing, and his death, per the Metropolitan Police Department and the U.S. Attorney's Office's public findings.

The two men who restrained Smith were "special police officers" — privately employed, armed security personnel licensed by the District with limited arrest powers, distinct from sworn Metropolitan Police officers.
The D.C. Chief Medical Examiner classified Smith's manner of death as homicide, while also finding cocaine intoxication and cardiac arrest were contributing factors.

The U.S. Attorney's Office announced in October 2016, after a review including body camera footage, autopsy and toxicology reports, and interviews with more than two dozen witnesses, that there was insufficient evidence to prove the officers used excessive force or possessed criminal intent.
An initial police report characterized the incident as a "justifiable homicide" before D.C. police said that classification was an error and changed it to a standard death investigation.
The identities of the two special police officers involved have never been publicly released, and the private security company that employed them has not been named in most public reporting.
unknown: Whether the level of force used to restrain Smith — including what witnesses described as an officer's knee on his back — independently caused or substantially contributed to his death, versus the cocaine intoxication prosecutors emphasized, was never resolved by any criminal proceeding.
Why the two special police officers involved have never been publicly named, even after the U.S. Attorney's Office concluded its investigation, has not been explained in available public reporting.
The full body camera footage capturing the incident was only partially released to the public, limiting independent review of the restraint itself.
unanswered: Why have the special police officers involved in Smith's death never been publicly identified, even after the criminal investigation concluded?
What oversight, if any, exists for the roughly 7,000-plus privately employed special police officers operating with arrest powers across Washington, D.C.?
Why did the original police report classify the incident as a "justifiable homicide" before that classification was retracted as an error?

sources.name: U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. — official statement on the Alonzo Smith investigation
FOX 5 DC — “Security guards will not be charged in death of Alonzo Smith”
The Washington Post — “Family demands to know why D.C. man was in custody of 'special police,' and how he died”

name: Darius Tarver
summary: Darius Tarver, 23, a University of North Texas criminal justice student and member of the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement, was shot and killed by a Denton, Texas police officer on January 21, 2020, outside his apartment. Just a week earlier, Tarver had suffered a traumatic brain injury in a car crash and been released from the ICU; his family said he began exhibiting significant mental impairment afterward. His roommate called police for help after Tarver barricaded himself in his room, muttering about God and light. Body camera video showed him holding a frying pan and a large knife when four officers arrived; after he was Tased twice without effect and continued to advance, one officer opened fire. A Denton County grand jury declined to indict the officer, whose name was never publicly released, in March 2021. An internal department review separately found no policy violations. No one has ever been charged in Tarver's death.
known: Tarver's traumatic brain injury the week before, his roommate's 911 call for help, and the shooting itself, per Denton Police Department body camera footage and public statements.

Four officers responded to the scene; Tarver was Tased twice without apparent effect before an officer fired the fatal shots as he advanced holding a frying pan and knife, per police accounts of the body camera footage.

Denton Police Chief Frank Dixon stated at a March 2020 news conference that officers were "clearly under threat" and suggested Tarver may have been under the influence of drugs; Tarver's family disputed that account, attributing his behavior to the brain injury.
A Denton County grand jury declined to indict the involved officer, whose identity police never publicly released, on March 18, 2021 — 14 months after the shooting.

Denton's internal affairs investigation concluded the officers followed department training, procedures, and policy given the totality of the circumstances, and no officer faced any disciplinary action.

Following Tarver's death, the Denton Police Department created a dedicated mental health response division, which his father, a police chaplain in a neighboring city, said was a positive but insufficient outcome.
A petition organized by Tarver's father calling for criminal charges, an independent special prosecutor, and a Department of Justice investigation gathered nearly 200,000 signatures.
unknown: Whether Tarver's continued advance after being Tased twice reflected the imminent threat the department maintained, or a disoriented reaction consistent with a recent traumatic brain injury, as his family argued, was never tested at any criminal trial.
Why the involved officer's identity has never been publicly released, even after the grand jury and internal investigation both concluded, is not explained in available public reporting.

Whether responding officers had specific crisis-intervention training for encounters involving a recent traumatic brain injury, as opposed to general mental health crisis training, has not been detailed publicly.
unanswered: Why did four responding officers, aware they were facing someone in an active mental health crisis, not attempt additional de-escalation before the situation reached lethal force?
Why has the involved officer's identity never been publicly disclosed, even after both the grand jury and internal review concluded?
What specific outcomes has Denton's newly created mental health response division achieved in the years since Tarver's death?

sources.name: The Dallas Morning News — “Denton officer won't face charges in fatal shooting of UNT student Darius Tarver”
Dallas Observer — “Denton Police Who Killed Darius Tarver Won't be Charged, Sparking Outrage”

name: Chinedu Okobi
summary: Chinedu Okobi, 36, a Morehouse College graduate and father, died on October 3, 2018 after San Mateo County, California sheriff's deputies Tased him repeatedly, struck him with a baton, and pepper-sprayed him during a confrontation that began when a deputy approached him for jaywalking on El Camino Real in Millbrae. Okobi crossed the street to get away from the deputy; when more deputies arrived, a violent struggle followed in which he was shocked with a Taser seven times. He went into cardiac arrest and died; an autopsy attributed his death to cardiac arrest linked to an undiagnosed enlarged heart, physical exertion, restraint, and the repeated Taser shocks. San Mateo County District Attorney Steve Wagstaffe announced in March 2019 that none of the five deputies and sergeant involved would face criminal charges. Okobi was the third person with mental illness to die after being Tased by law enforcement in San Mateo County within that same year. No one has ever been charged in Okobi's death.
known: The jaywalking stop, the struggle, and the repeated Taser deployments, per video released by the San Mateo County District Attorney's office and Wagstaffe's own public findings.

Deputy Joshua Wang initially approached Okobi for jaywalking; when Okobi crossed the street away from him, additional deputies were called and a struggle followed involving batons, pepper spray, and multiple Taser deployments — seven by most reporting, though the exact count varies slightly across sources.

An autopsy found Okobi died of cardiac arrest, with an undiagnosed enlarged heart identified as a contributing risk factor for sudden death following Taser shocks, a risk a UCSF cardiac researcher testified applies broadly to repeated Taser use.

District Attorney Steve Wagstaffe announced on March 1, 2019 that none of the four deputies or the sergeant present would face criminal charges, calling the death a "horrible tragedy" while declining to fault Okobi.

None of the deputies present turned Okobi onto his side, as department policy required after restraint, and none administered CPR before paramedics arrived, according to a local news account of the incident.
San Mateo County's own internal affairs investigation later cleared the deputies of policy violations as well.
In 2023, San Mateo County agreed to pay Okobi's family $4.5 million to settle a wrongful death lawsuit.
unknown: Whether the level of force used — seven Taser deployments combined with baton strikes and pepper spray against a man who deputies acknowledged never displayed a weapon — was proportionate to the threat he posed was disputed by the family's attorney, who called it "over-aggressiveness," and was never tested at any criminal trial.

Why none of the deputies present repositioned Okobi onto his side or began CPR before paramedics arrived, despite department policy, was not directly addressed in the district attorney's public charging decision.

The precise sequence connecting the initial jaywalking stop to the level of force ultimately used has been described somewhat differently across the district attorney's account and the family's characterization of the video.
unanswered: Why did an initial jaywalking stop escalate to seven Taser deployments, baton strikes, and pepper spray against a man deputies never described as armed?
Why did none of the deputies present provide CPR or reposition Okobi as department policy required once he became unresponsive?
What connects this case to the two other Taser-related deaths of people with mental illness in San Mateo County that same year, and what departmental review, if any, addressed that pattern?

San Francisco Chronicle — “Chinedu Okobi case: San Mateo sheriff's deputies cleared in Taser death of unarmed black man”

name: Osaze Osagie
summary: Osaze Osagie, 29, who had schizophrenia and Asperger's syndrome, was shot and killed by a State College, Pennsylvania police officer on March 20, 2019, at his apartment while three officers attempted to serve a mental health warrant his own father had requested. Sylvester Osagie, worried about his son's deteriorating condition, had asked police for an involuntary commitment warrant after his son sent a text threatening self-harm. When officers arrived, Osagie reportedly ran at them holding a steak knife; one officer fired three shots, striking him once in the shoulder and twice in the back as he turned. It was the first fatal police shooting in the department's 103-year history. Centre County District Attorney Bernie Cantorna announced in May 2019, after a six-week investigation, that the officer would face no charges, finding the shooting justified. A federal judge dismissed the family's civil lawsuit in 2023. No one has ever been charged in Osagie's death.
known: Sylvester Osagie's request for a mental health warrant, the officers' response, and the shooting, per the Pennsylvania State Police investigative report and the Centre County District Attorney's public findings.

All three responding officers had completed 40-hour Crisis Intervention Team training, described by the borough as the "gold standard" for police response to mental health situations; one officer was additionally trained by the FBI as a crisis negotiator.

The officers were given a copy of Osagie's text message threatening self-harm before responding, but the DA's report noted no other information about his prior legal or health history was made available to them, and they did not develop a specific joint plan before engaging him.

District Attorney Bernie Cantorna announced on May 8, 2019 that the shooting was legally justified and that the officer, whose identity was never publicly released per standard department and state police practice for uncharged shootings, acted in defense of himself and a fellow officer.

U.S. Middle District Judge Matthew Brann dismissed the family's federal lawsuit in November 2023 on summary judgment, ruling the officers, who were not mental health professionals, could not be held liable "for failing to be something they are not, and a death they did not cause."

The shooting prompted the formation of a local mental health task force, which issued 21 recommendations in November 2020; as of four years after Osagie's death, only seven had been implemented, and advocates said removing firearms from officers serving mental health warrants was never seriously considered.
unknown: Whether Osagie's advance with the knife presented the imminent threat that justified deadly force, given he was fatally struck twice in the back — suggesting he may have been turning away at the moment of at least some shots — was disputed by community members reviewing the same investigative findings and was never resolved at any criminal trial.

Why officers with specialized crisis intervention and hostage-negotiation training did not develop a specific de-escalation plan before engaging Osagie has not been fully explained beyond the DA's report noting that gap occurred.

Whether Pennsylvania's mental health warrant process, which the DA himself said should change, has been meaningfully reformed regarding whether armed police officers must be the ones serving such warrants remains disputed by local advocates.
unanswered: Why did specially trained crisis-intervention and hostage-negotiation officers not develop a coordinated de-escalation plan before approaching a man they knew to be suicidal?
Why were two of the three fatal shots to Osagie's back, and how does that square with the DA's finding that the officer faced an ongoing frontal threat?

Why has implementation of the local mental health task force's 21 recommendations remained slow years after Osagie's death, and why was removing firearms from the 302 warrant process never seriously considered?

WITF — “DA: No Charges for police shooting in State College”
StateCollege.com — “Federal Judge Dismisses Osagie Family Lawsuit Against State College, Police Officers”

name: Julian Lewis
summary: Julian Edward Roosevelt Lewis, 60, a semi-retired carpenter, was shot in the face and killed by Georgia State Patrol Trooper Jacob Thompson on a rural road in Screven County, Georgia, on August 7, 2020, after Thompson tried to stop him over a broken taillight. When Lewis did not immediately stop, Thompson performed a PIT maneuver that forced his car into a ditch, then shot him once, unarmed, within about two seconds of getting out of his own patrol car. Thompson wrote in his report that Lewis had been revving his engine and turning the wheel as if trying to ram him — a claim a Georgia Bureau of Investigation agent later testified was physically impossible, since the crash had disconnected Lewis's car battery, leaving the vehicle inoperable. Thompson was fired and charged with felony murder days later, but a Screven County grand jury declined to indict him in June 2021. No one has ever been convicted in Lewis's death.
known: The traffic stop for a broken taillight, the PIT maneuver, and the shooting, per the Georgia State Patrol's own incident report and subsequent Georgia Bureau of Investigation findings.
A GBI agent testified that Thompson fired his weapon approximately two seconds after exiting his patrol car.

Thompson's written account stated Lewis revved his engine and turned his wheel as if attempting to ram him; a GBI agent testified in court that this was impossible, since Lewis's car battery had disconnected when his vehicle hit the ditch, rendering it inoperable.

Thompson, a 27-year-old white trooper who had joined the Georgia State Patrol in 2013, was fired and arrested on charges of felony murder and aggravated assault on August 14, 2020, one week after the shooting.
A Screven County judge initially denied Thompson bail given "the factual circumstances of the case," though he was later released on $100,000 bond in December 2020.

A 22-person Screven County grand jury declined to indict Thompson in June 2021, after hearing his own testimony — a practice Georgia law permits for current or former law enforcement — and considering Georgia's self-defense statutes.

Following the grand jury's decision, Lewis's family and attorneys led a 63-mile march to Savannah, after which federal prosecutors announced they were examining the case "in consultation with the FBI"; no subsequent public announcement of federal charges has been reported.
unknown: Whether Thompson perceived a genuine threat at the moment he fired, despite the GBI's finding that Lewis's account of the car's condition was physically impossible, was the central issue for the grand jury and was never resolved by any conviction.
Why the grand jury declined to indict despite the GBI's own contradiction of Thompson's central justification has never been explained, since grand jury deliberations are sealed under Georgia law.

Whether the Ogeechee Judicial Circuit District Attorney's office ever attempted to present the case to a second grand jury, and the ultimate outcome of the federal review opened after the family's march to Savannah, have not been consistently reported in later public sources.
unanswered: How did a grand jury decline to indict when the state's own investigative agency had already contradicted the trooper's central account of the shooting?
What became of the federal investigation opened by the U.S. Attorney's office following the Lewis family's 63-mile march to Savannah?
Why was Thompson permitted to testify directly to the grand jury under Georgia's law allowing law enforcement that privilege, and how did his testimony affect the outcome?

WSAV-TV — “No indictment for former Georgia trooper in death of Julian Lewis”
AP, via Yahoo News — “Feds 'examining' shooting of Black man by Georgia trooper”

name: Emantic “E.J.” Bradford Jr.
summary: Emantic “E.J.” Bradford Jr., 21, was shot three times from behind and killed by Hoover, Alabama Police Officer David Alexander at the Riverchase Galleria mall on Thanksgiving night, November 22, 2018, moments after another man opened fire during an altercation, wounding an 18-year-old and a 12-year-old bystander. Bradford, who held a valid permit to carry, was seen on surveillance video running toward the wounded with his gun drawn; witnesses and his family's attorney said he was trying to help, not attack anyone. Hoover police initially publicly identified Bradford himself as the shooter, then retracted that within a day. Alabama's attorney general took over the case from the local district attorney, citing conflicts of interest, and announced in February 2019 that the officer had mistakenly believed Bradford fired the earlier shots but was still legally justified in killing him regardless. The FBI separately found no basis for federal civil rights charges. No one has ever been charged in Bradford's death.
known: The mall altercation, the earlier gunfire that wounded two bystanders, and Bradford's shooting, per Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall's public report and released surveillance video.
Bradford held a valid Alabama permit to carry the firearm found on him.
An independent autopsy commissioned by Bradford's family found he was struck three times from behind, in the head, neck, and back.

Hoover police publicly identified Bradford as the shooter the night of the incident, then retracted that identification, then retracted a follow-up claim that he had brandished a weapon at officers, before the actual gunman, Erron Brown, was later arrested and charged separately.

Attorney General Marshall's February 2019 report concluded the officer mistakenly believed Bradford was the shooter but was nonetheless legally justified, since Bradford was armed and the officer's duty was to “eliminate the threat” he perceived.
The FBI reviewed the matter and found no evidence to support federal civil rights charges against the officer, per the Attorney General's office.
The shooting prompted weeks of sustained protests in Hoover, including demonstrations outside City Hall demanding release of body camera and surveillance footage.
unknown: Whether the officer had a reasonable opportunity to identify Bradford as someone helping the wounded, rather than the shooter, before firing has been disputed by the family's attorney, Ben Crump, who called the investigation a “cover-up,” and was never tested at any criminal trial.

The involved officer's identity, later reported as David Alexander per Wikipedia's sourced case history, was not initially released by Hoover police or the Attorney General's office in their own public statements.
The full, unedited body camera footage from the officer who fired was not among the surveillance video the Attorney General's office released publicly.
unanswered: Why did Hoover police publicly identify Bradford as the shooter, then retract that claim, then retract a second claim that he brandished a weapon at officers, all within days of the shooting?
Why has the officer's body camera footage, as opposed to mall surveillance video, never been made public?
What accountability, if any, exists when an officer's mistaken belief about who fired the initial shots is treated as sufficient justification for killing an unrelated armed bystander?

NBC News — “Alabama officer's fatal shooting of 21-year-old at mall was 'justified,' state says”
CNN — “Alabama attorney general takes over mall shooting cases, citing conflicts of interest”

name: Kayla Moore
summary: Kayla Moore, 41, a Black transgender woman living with schizophrenia, died in Berkeley, California police custody on February 12, 2013, after up to six officers restrained her face-down on a futon in her own apartment. Her roommate had called police asking for a mental health welfare check, not an arrest; officers instead learned of an outstanding warrant — later found to have actually been issued for a different person who shared her legal name — and moved to take her into custody. During the struggle to restrain her, Moore stopped breathing and could not be revived. A Berkeley police sergeant's internal report ruled the death accidental and the force used reasonable within three months. No criminal charges were ever sought against any officer. A federal judge dismissed the family's civil rights lawsuit in 2016, and the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that dismissal in 2020, finding the officers had not used excessive force. No one has ever been held accountable in Moore's death.
known: The welfare-check call, the restraint, and Moore's death, per the Berkeley Police Department's own internal report and the Alameda County coroner's findings.
Moore's roommate called police specifically requesting a mental health evaluation, not an arrest, after she became agitated during a psychotic episode.
The warrant officers used to justify arresting Moore was later determined to have been issued for a different person who happened to share her legal first name, per the family's civil complaint.
Up to six officers restrained Moore face-down, applying body weight to her limbs and back; a spit hood was readied but never used before she stopped breathing.
Berkeley Police Sergeant Peter Hong's internal report, released about three months later, ruled Moore's death accidental and the force used by officers reasonable.
The Alameda County coroner found potentially toxic levels of methamphetamine and codeine in Moore's system, along with obesity and an enlarged heart, as contributing factors.

U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer granted summary judgment for the officers in 2016, finding their use of force reasonable; a separate Americans with Disabilities Act claim was dismissed in 2018 for insufficient evidence.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal in January 2020, ruling that while Moore's death was a tragedy, the officers had not acted unlawfully based on the evidence presented.
unknown: Whether officers reasonably should have recognized that restraining Moore face-down under the combined weight of up to six people risked impairing her breathing was central to the family's claims and was addressed differently by the internal police review versus the family's own expert accounts, but was never resolved by any criminal proceeding since none was brought.

The family separately alleged officers made discriminatory remarks about Moore's gender identity and declined to promptly administer CPR because of it; this claim was not specifically resolved in the courts' published rulings on the excessive-force and ADA claims.
Why the arrest proceeded on a warrant later found to belong to a different person, before that discrepancy was caught, has not been fully explained in public reporting.
unanswered: Why was Moore arrested on a warrant that was later found to belong to someone else entirely, and what verification steps, if any, failed?

Did the responding officers' handling of Moore's care immediately after she stopped breathing meet department protocol, and was that specifically reviewed apart from the broader excessive-force finding?
What has become of Berkeley's policies for responding to mental-health-crisis calls involving transgender residents since Moore's death?

sources.name: KQED — “Berkeley Death in Police Custody Was Accidental, Probe Concludes”
San Francisco Chronicle — “Berkeley officers didn't use excessive force against transgender woman, appeals court rules”
Courthouse News Service — “Judge Clears Berkeley Police in Woman's Death”

name: Steven Taylor
summary: Steven Taylor, 33, was shot and killed by San Leandro, California Police Officer Jason Fletcher inside a Walmart on April 18, 2020, after being reported for shoplifting while holding an aluminum baseball bat. Body camera video showed that within about 40 seconds of Fletcher's arrival, he Tased Taylor twice and then fired a single fatal round into his chest; Taylor's family said he was suffering a mental health crisis, not posing a deadly threat. Fletcher was charged with voluntary manslaughter in 2021, becoming a rare case of an officer criminally charged in California for an on-duty shooting. After more than five years of delays, prosecutorial turnover, and disputes over withheld evidence, Alameda County's district attorney moved to drop the charges in December 2025, and a judge dismissed the case just weeks before it was finally set to go to trial. No one has ever been convicted in Taylor's death.
known: The shoplifting report, the confrontation, and the shooting, per San Leandro Police Department body camera footage and the Alameda County District Attorney's charging and dismissal filings.
Fletcher deployed his Taser twice against Taylor before firing a single round into his chest, all within roughly 40 seconds of arriving on scene.
Then-District Attorney Nancy O'Malley charged Fletcher with voluntary manslaughter in June 2021.

The case was delayed for years amid multiple changes in Alameda County's district attorney's office, including recalled DA Pamela Price's tenure, during which Fletcher's attorney alleged use-of-force expert opinions favorable to the defense were withheld from the case record.
A judge denied an earlier defense motion to dismiss the case in November 2025, ruling a jury should weigh the disputed evidence and allowing the case to proceed toward trial.

Weeks later, in December 2025, District Attorney Ursula Jones Dickson's office filed its own motion to drop the charges, stating prosecutors could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Fletcher had committed a crime or that he had not acted in lawful self-defense; a judge granted that dismissal on December 12, 2025.

Taylor's family and community advocates, including his grandmother Addie Kitchen and the Anti-Police Terror Project's Cat Brooks, publicly said Fletcher had other options, including de-escalating or waiting for personnel trained in mental health crisis response.
unknown: Whether Taylor's continued movement with the bat after being Tased twice constituted the kind of imminent deadly threat that legally justified Fletcher's shot, or whether de-escalation and additional time remained available, was the central dispute of the case and was never resolved by a jury, since it never reached trial.

The specific use-of-force expert opinions that Fletcher's attorney alleged were withheld from the defense during a prior district attorney's tenure, and how directly they shaped the final dismissal, have been described by competing parties but not independently verified in a public record.
Whether Taylor's documented mental health history was known to responding officers before or during the encounter has not been detailed in the available public charging and dismissal filings.
unanswered: Why did it take more than five years, and multiple changes in district attorneys, for this case to be resolved without ever reaching a jury?
What specific use-of-force expert opinions were allegedly withheld from Fletcher's defense, and by whom, during the case's years-long delay?
What has the San Leandro Police Department changed, if anything, about how officers respond to reported mental health crises since Taylor's death?

San Francisco Chronicle — “Ex-San Leandro officer's case dismissed in fatal 2020 Walmart shooting”
