name: De'Von Bailey
summary: De'Von Bailey, 19, was shot and killed by Colorado Springs Police Officers Blake Evenson and Sgt. Alan Van't Land on August 3, 2019, while running away from officers investigating a report of an armed robbery. Body camera video, later released publicly, showed officers firing eight shots total, striking Bailey three times in the back and once in the arm as he fled; officers said he had reached for a firearm, but the released footage does not clearly show him pulling a weapon from his pocket before the shooting began. A gun was recovered at the scene. Fourth Judicial District Attorney Dan May referred the case to a grand jury rather than deciding himself, and in November 2019 the grand jury found the officers' use of force justified, declining to indict either of them. The city later paid Bailey's family nearly $3 million to settle a federal civil rights lawsuit alleging racial profiling, without admitting wrongdoing. No one has ever been charged in Bailey's death.
known: The robbery investigation, the foot pursuit, and the shooting, per Colorado Springs Police Department body camera footage released to the public in August 2019.
Officers fired eight shots total, striking Bailey three times in the back and once in the arm as he ran; a firearm was recovered at the scene.

District Attorney Dan May referred the case to a grand jury rather than making a charging decision himself, a choice Bailey family attorney Mari Newman publicly said was designed to avoid a prosecutorial indictment.

The grand jury, whose members' identities were not disclosed, heard from the two officers and a use-of-force expert before declining to indict either officer in November 2019, releasing a public report stating Bailey's own actions led the officers to use deadly force.
Bailey's parents filed a federal civil rights lawsuit alleging officers racially profiled their son and assumed, partly because of his race, that he presented an enhanced threat.
The City of Colorado Springs settled that lawsuit for nearly $3 million in 2022, explicitly stating the settlement was not an admission of wrongdoing and noting the grand jury's earlier finding.
unknown: Whether Bailey in fact reached for or pulled the recovered firearm before officers opened fire, as they maintained, has been disputed by the family's attorneys, who say the released video does not clearly show that action occurring before the shots were fired, and was never resolved at any criminal trial.
The specific reasoning behind the grand jury's finding, beyond its public report's general conclusion, has not been made available given Colorado's grand jury secrecy rules.

The extent to which race played a role in officers' split-second assessment of Bailey as an enhanced threat, as the family's federal complaint alleged, was never adjudicated on the merits since the case settled before trial.
unanswered: Why does the body camera footage not clearly show Bailey drawing a weapon before officers opened fire, despite that being the central justification given for the shooting?
Why did the district attorney choose to refer the case to a grand jury rather than make an independent charging decision, and did that choice affect the outcome, as the family's attorney alleged?
What did the city's nearly $3 million settlement reflect about the racial profiling allegations in the family's lawsuit, given it explicitly disclaimed any admission of wrongdoing?

name: Antwon Rose II
summary: Antwon Rose II, 17, was shot three times — in the back, arm, and side of the face — and killed by East Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Police Officer Michael Rosfeld on June 19, 2018, as he ran from a car that had been pulled over minutes after a drive-by shooting elsewhere. Rose, unarmed, fled along with another passenger while the driver was being arrested; bystander cellphone video captured the shooting. Rosfeld was charged with criminal homicide — he had been sworn in as an East Pittsburgh officer only hours before the shooting, following prior stints at other departments. At trial in March 2019, a jury that included three Black jurors deliberated fewer than four hours before acquitting Rosfeld of all charges, including first-degree murder, third-degree murder, voluntary manslaughter, and involuntary manslaughter. No one has ever been convicted in Rose's death.
known: The traffic stop, the flight, and the shooting, per Allegheny County court records and bystander cellphone video played at trial.
Rosfeld had been sworn in as an East Pittsburgh police officer only hours before the shooting; he had previously worked at other area police departments and as a University of Pittsburgh officer.

Rose was unarmed; police reported an empty ammunition magazine was found in his pocket and gunshot residue on his hand, consistent with the earlier drive-by shooting he was suspected of being involved in, though he himself fired no weapon during the traffic stop.
Allegheny County District Attorney Stephen Zappala charged Rosfeld with criminal homicide shortly after the shooting.
A jury of seven men and five women, including three Black jurors, deliberated fewer than four hours on March 22, 2019 before acquitting Rosfeld of all four possible charges.
Gunshots were fired into the office of Rosfeld's defense attorney the night after the acquittal; no one was injured.

East Pittsburgh's borough council voted to disband its police department entirely months after the shooting, citing cost and other factors; the department's contract with a regional force took effect in late 2018.
Allegheny County later paid an $8 million settlement to Rose's family in a related civil lawsuit.
unknown: Whether Rosfeld reasonably believed Rose posed a deadly threat as he fled unarmed was the central dispute at trial; the jury's acquittal reflects that it was not persuaded beyond a reasonable doubt of homicide, but the underlying factual dispute about what justified the shooting was never independently resolved beyond that verdict.
The specific reasoning behind the jury's under-four-hour deliberation, given the gravity of the charges, is not public, as with all jury deliberations.

Rose's own writing, including a poem publicly read by supporters after the verdict expressing his fears about how he might be perceived and treated by police, has been widely cited in public discussion of the case but is separate from the trial record itself.
unanswered: Why was Rosfeld sworn in as an East Pittsburgh officer only hours before the shooting, and what vetting, if any, preceded that appointment given his history at multiple prior departments?
Why did the jury acquit on all four possible charges, including involuntary manslaughter, after less than four hours of deliberation?
What became of East Pittsburgh's own police department following its dissolution months after the shooting, and did that decision reflect any accountability for how the department was run?

name: Angelo Crooms & Sincere Pierce
summary: Angelo “AJ” Crooms, 16, and Sincere Pierce, 18, were shot and killed by Brevard County, Florida Sheriff's Deputy Jafet Santiago-Miranda on November 13, 2020, in a Cocoa driveway during an attempted stop of a car deputies believed, based on a report that later proved incorrect, had been stolen. Dashcam video showed the deputy approaching with his gun drawn, repeatedly yelling for the car to stop; Crooms, who was driving, backed up slightly then drove forward, and the deputy opened fire, killing both teens. A third occupant survived uninjured. The family's attorneys said the video showed the car moving away from the deputy, not toward him, and that deputies never confirmed the car was actually stolen before drawing weapons. Brevard County State Attorney Phil Archer announced in April 2021 — the day after Derek Chauvin's murder conviction — that no charges would be filed. No one has ever been charged in either teen's death.
known: The attempted stop, the deputy's drawn weapon and verbal commands, and the shooting, per Brevard County Sheriff's Office dashcam video released publicly.

The car deputies pursued had been reported as possibly stolen; it was later established that report was incorrect, and the vehicle had been loaned to the teens by a family friend, per the family's attorneys.

Deputy Santiago-Miranda had previously been placed on administrative leave months earlier after allegedly threatening a person his wife was reportedly having an affair with, telling them they needed to “wear a bulletproof vest,” per records reviewed by Florida Today.

The Florida Department of Law Enforcement investigated and presented findings to the State Attorney's Office; State Attorney Phil Archer announced on April 21, 2021 that no criminal charges would be filed against the deputy.

Two guns were found in the car; the sheriff's office said it could not confirm who they belonged to or whether they were stolen, and the surviving third occupant was interviewed and released without charges.

Sincere Pierce's mother was accidentally shot and wounded by a 16-year-old attendee's discharging firearm during Pierce's own burial service on November 28, 2020, an unrelated tragedy that compounded the family's grief; his gravesite was separately vandalized months later.
unknown: Whether Crooms's car was in fact accelerating toward the deputy in a manner presenting a deadly threat, as the sheriff's office maintained, or moving away as the family's attorneys argued from the same dashcam footage, was never resolved at any criminal trial.
Why deputies approached the vehicle with weapons already drawn before confirming whether it was in fact stolen has not been fully explained in any official public accounting.
The full extent of Deputy Santiago-Miranda's prior disciplinary history beyond the reported administrative leave incident has not been made comprehensively public.
unanswered: Why did deputies approach the vehicle with guns already drawn before verifying the stolen-vehicle report that turned out to be incorrect?

Why did the State Attorney's announcement of no charges come specifically the day after a high-profile police murder conviction elsewhere, and did that timing reflect any broader pattern in how such decisions are announced?
What became of the investigation into who fired the gun that wounded Sincere Pierce's mother at his own burial?

name: Terrence Sterling
summary: Terrence Sterling, 31, was shot and killed by Metropolitan Police Department Officer Brian Trainer in Washington, D.C. in the early morning hours of September 11, 2016, after officers blocked his motorcycle with their cruiser following a high-speed chase. Trainer said Sterling revved his motorcycle and rammed it into the cruiser's door, pinning his leg, forcing him to fire twice through the window; an internal MPD investigator later testified he doubted Trainer's account, and the department's own review board found Trainer was not in danger and had no reason to draw his weapon at all. Trainer had not activated his body camera until one to three minutes after the shooting, violating department policy. Federal prosecutors declined to bring charges in August 2017. D.C.'s MPD trial board recommended firing Trainer months later for the unjustified shooting, and the police chief fired him in 2018 after his appeal was denied — an administrative outcome, not a criminal one. No one has ever been criminally charged in Sterling's death.
known: The chase, the cruiser blocking Sterling's path, and the shooting, per the U.S. Attorney's Office's public statement and subsequent MPD internal review findings.

Sterling had been driving erratically and at high speed, reaching over 100 mph at times and running red lights, before officers caught up to him; his autopsy found a blood alcohol level twice the legal limit and marijuana in his system.
Trainer did not activate his body camera until one to three minutes after the shooting, in violation of department policy.

An MPD internal affairs investigator testified to the department's trial board that he did not believe Trainer sustained the leg injury he described from the motorcycle striking the cruiser door, instead believing it occurred while Trainer was attempting to render aid to Sterling afterward.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia announced in August 2017 that there was insufficient evidence to prove Trainer had violated Sterling's civil rights with the necessary criminal intent, declining federal or D.C. charges; per a 2016 study cited by The Washington Post, no D.C. police officer had ever been criminally indicted for a fatal on-duty shooting.

MPD's own internal review, obtained by The Washington Post in December 2017, found Trainer had no reason to pull his gun and was not in danger when he fired, directly contradicting his account; a department trial board recommended his firing, and Police Chief Peter Newsham terminated him in June 2018 after denying his appeal.
The District of Columbia settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Sterling's family for $3.5 million, described at the time as the largest such payout in the city's history.
unknown: Whether Sterling intentionally rammed the cruiser door, as Trainer maintained, or whether the collision occurred differently, was disputed by the department's own internal investigator and trial board, and was never resolved by any criminal proceeding since none was brought.

Why federal prosecutors concluded the evidence was insufficient for criminal charges when the department's own internal review reached the opposite conclusion about whether the shooting was justified has not been reconciled in any single public accounting.

The specific content of witness Howard Dorsey's account, which Trainer's attorneys and prosecutors weighed differently in reaching their respective conclusions, has been described inconsistently across public reporting.
unanswered: Why did federal prosecutors decline charges when the police department's own internal review found the shooting unjustified and contradicted the officer's account?
What changes, if any, did MPD make to its body-camera activation enforcement following this case's documented policy violation?
Why has no D.C. police officer ever been criminally indicted for a fatal on-duty shooting, according to the city's own cited study, and has that pattern held since Sterling's case?

name: Jamee Johnson
summary: Jamee Johnson, 22, a Florida A&M University student, was shot and killed by Jacksonville Sheriff's Officer Josue Garriga during a traffic stop for a seatbelt violation on December 14, 2019. Body camera footage showed Johnson telling Garriga he had a legally owned handgun in the car; after Garriga asked him to step out, Johnson dove back into the vehicle, a struggle followed, and Garriga shot him four times, with video capturing Johnson begging for his life. Garriga said Johnson was reaching for the gun; the family's attorney argued the autopsy's bullet trajectories contradicted that account. Florida's State Attorney's Office concluded in July 2020 that the shooting was justified, declining to bring charges. The city later settled a federal civil lawsuit with Johnson's family for $200,000, without admitting wrongdoing. In 2024, Garriga was separately arrested and charged with child sex crimes unrelated to the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Johnson's death.
known: The traffic stop, the struggle, and the shooting, per State Attorney's Office body camera footage and its published investigation report.
Johnson told Garriga at the start of the stop that he had a firearm in the car; he did not have a concealed carry permit.

Garriga stated Johnson dove back into the car, then began lifting the firearm toward his face during the struggle, and that he fired after freeing himself from the vehicle, fearing Johnson still had the gun.
The State Attorney's Office released its investigation report and the body camera footage publicly in July 2020, concluding the shooting was justified and declining to file charges.

The family's attorney, Harry Daniels, argued that autopsy findings showing Johnson was struck left-to-right contradicted Garriga's account of the shooting's sequence and positioning, and that video showed Johnson exiting the car with his hands raised before the fatal shots.

The City of Jacksonville settled the family's federal civil rights lawsuit for $200,000 in 2023, without admitting Garriga did anything wrong, citing the uncertainty of a trial; the family had originally sought $5 million.
In 2024, Garriga, who had since left the department, was arrested on unrelated charges of child sex crimes in Clay County, Florida — a case entirely separate from the Johnson shooting.
unknown: Whether Johnson was in fact reaching for or holding the firearm at the moment Garriga fired, as Garriga maintained, or whether physical evidence contradicts that account, as the family's attorney argued based on the autopsy's bullet trajectories, was never tested at any criminal trial.

The specific reasoning behind the State Attorney's Office's justified-shooting finding, beyond its published report, has been publicly disputed by the family's attorney but not independently re-examined by any other authority.

Whether Garriga's later, unrelated arrest reflects anything about his conduct or character at the time of the 2019 shooting has not been established and is a separate matter the State Attorney's investigation did not address.
unanswered: Why does the family's attorney say the autopsy's bullet trajectories contradict Garriga's account of how the shooting unfolded?
Why did the City of Jacksonville settle the family's lawsuit for a fraction of what was sought, and did that reflect any assessment of the underlying facts?
What connection, if any, exists between this case and the pattern the family and local commentators have pointed to regarding Jacksonville's use-of-force review process more broadly?

name: Dreasjon “Sean” Reed
summary: Dreasjon “Sean” Reed, 21, a former U.S. Air Force airman and legal gun owner, was shot and killed by Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department Officer Dejoure Mercer on May 6, 2020, at the end of a high-speed chase Reed livestreamed on Facebook to thousands of viewers in real time. The chase itself had been called off by IMPD's own chief for being too dangerous; Mercer, on foot, caught up to Reed after he parked and ran. The livestream's shaky camera captured the sound of a Taser and then gunshots, but never showed the shooting itself clearly, and no body camera or dashcam footage of the moment existed. Police said Reed fired at Mercer first; his family's attorney said he never had a gun in his hand at all. A detective who later walked past Reed's body was recorded joking it would be a “closed casket” and was internally disciplined for it. A special grand jury declined to indict Mercer in November 2020, six months after the shooting. No one has ever been charged in Reed's death.
known: The chase, the foot pursuit, and the shooting, per IMPD statements and Reed's own Facebook Live video, which was watched by thousands as it happened.

IMPD Deputy Chief Kendale Adams's pursuit of Reed on the interstate was called off by supervisors roughly 10 minutes in for being too dangerous; Officer Mercer separately spotted Reed's parked car and continued the pursuit on foot alone.
No body camera or dashcam footage of the shooting itself exists; the only contemporaneous recording is Reed's own Facebook Live stream, whose camera did not capture the shooting clearly.

Police said Reed and Mercer exchanged gunfire and that a gun found near Reed had likely been fired twice; the family's attorney stated at a press conference that Reed “did not shoot a gun, did not point a gun, did not brandish a gun at an officer.”
A separate officer at the scene was recorded on another device joking that Reed's death would require a “closed casket”; IMPD disciplined that officer following public backlash.
Special Prosecutor Rosemary Khoury convened a six-person special grand jury, which returned a “no bill” on November 10, 2020, finding insufficient probable cause to indict Mercer.
Reed's death was the first of three separate fatal police encounters in Indianapolis within roughly 24 hours that month, prompting sustained protests across the city.
Reed's family filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the city, IMPD, the police chief, and the involved officers.
unknown: Whether Reed in fact fired at or pointed a weapon toward Mercer, as police maintained, or never held a gun during the confrontation, as the family's attorney stated, was never resolved by any criminal trial, and the shooting itself was not captured on any camera.

Surveillance footage later obtained by local reporters reportedly showed Reed running with a t-shirt in one hand and cell phones in the other in the moments before the confrontation, which the family's attorney cited as inconsistent with him also holding and firing a weapon; how that footage was weighed by the grand jury is not public.
The full reasoning behind the grand jury's no-bill decision has not been made public, as Indiana grand jury proceedings are sealed.
unanswered: Given that no body camera or dashcam footage captured the shooting itself, what specific evidence did the grand jury rely on to conclude there was insufficient probable cause to indict?
Why did an officer feel comfortable making a “closed casket” joke at the scene of a shooting his own department was actively investigating, and what discipline resulted beyond an internal reprimand?
What became of the Reed family's federal civil rights lawsuit against the city and IMPD?
